articles.title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Had a Relationship With a Second Employee
articles.body:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Had a Relationship With a Second Employee (techcrunch.com) 82
			
		 	
				Reuters reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a third woman (source paywalled; alternative source ), an unnamed Nvidia employee. The revelation follows reports of two other extramarital affairs: one with Nvidia VP Kimberly Powell and another with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects of being a Chinese spy. The latter relationship has also prompted a shareholder lawsuit alleging Nvidia misled investors about its ties to a company suspected of circumventing U.S. chip export restrictions. Jensen Huang has since resigned as Nvidia's CEO and stepped down from its board on Thursday. CFO Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO 136
			
		 	
				Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia after 33 years leading the company, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said board chair Harvey Jones in a release announcing the news.
The abrupt departure follows revelations about Huang's affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was a Chinese spy. CNBC reports:  Huang, 63, apologized on Sunday for being "unfaithful to my wife," though he provided no details about the affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who has worked for a Chinese company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Late Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia CEO also had a separate affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at the chipmaker. Later that afternoon The Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia's board met to discuss the company's future.
Jensen Huang denied allegations that he had compromised national security or Nvidia secrets after reports of the Alice Huang affair. The news sparked concerns that Nvidia knew companies based in Singapore and Malaysia had been evading U.S. export controls in accessing its technology. The board said on Tuesday that it had hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate the intelligence allegations.

articles.title: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
articles.body:
Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found.
AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
A study testing Gemini, Perplexity, and ChatGPT found that in as many as 15 percent of conversations, chatbots displayed ‘risky’ URLs.
The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of 151 brands. Questions included “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?”; “Where can I find [brand] online?”; and “Does [brand] ship internationally? What are their regional websites?” The test ran over the course of two testing periods in September and asked about 151 small and large companies like fashion brands Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, and Madhappy (a client of Podqi) and homeware brand Le Creuset. Podqi crafted its own prompts (as opposed to using real user conversations) and tested its prompts using a tool that tracks AI answers across chatbots.
Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers
Over the course of 6,795 answers, Podqi found that all three AI engines cited and showed shoppers risky sites, defined as fake websites impersonating real retailers or selling knockoffs, old brand domains that have been reregistered by someone else, or dead sites that aren’t active at all but that someone else could purchase and reuse. Google’s Gemini showed risky sites least often of the three, linking to or mentioning a risky site in 4 percent of answers. (Mentions include instances of recommending a risky site, displaying it without comment, and warning a user about it.) Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers. ChatGPT fell somewhere in the middle at 8 percent. ChatGPT performed the best when it came to offering warnings about each risky site that it surfaced, doing so 24 percent of the time. Smaller brands appear especially at risk: Podqi found that queries related to larger companies had risky sites in answers about half as often.
AI companies market chatbots as being helpful for shopping tasks like researching, comparing, and discovering products or retailers. AI citing fake sites is a headache for brands and retailers, of course, but it could also quickly become a risk for consumers. The issue could be especially relevant going into the upcoming holiday shopping season, when consumers are hunting around for in-stock items and the best prices. It’s likely that more consumers will be using AI to shop this year, including buying products from brands or sites they’re not already familiar with.
“Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” says Podqi CEO and cofounder Trevor West.
“We take information quality seriously, and are happy to see that Gemini performed best among the products tested,” Google spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said in an email. “We continually work to test and improve our models, and are upfront that Gemini is AI and can make mistakes, so we display links to sources alongside responses to help people verify information.”
“Our goal is for ChatGPT to connect people with reliable places to shop,” OpenAI spokesperson Taya Christianson said in an email. “We’re continuing to improve our safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping-related results. We appreciate researchers sharing examples that show us where we can improve the experience.”
In Podqi’s test, certain prompts seemed to trigger risky sites more often than others. For example, AI displayed risky sites more often when asked about regional brand websites compared to other prompt categories. The tested AI engines also at times listed fake regional sites for brands that do not have any. In one conversation, Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy’s official website and called it “the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items.”
“Perplexity is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, and has been for four years. We never claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company relentlessly focused on it,” spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said in an email.

articles.title: Easy Homemade Cornbread
articles.body:
Cornbread is a highly underrated side dish. You can whip up this deliciously sweet and moist Homemade Cornbread recipe with just a few pantry staples, and it makes a perfect side dish for breakfast, lunch, or dinner! Serve it slathered with butter at breakfast, crumbled into your soup or chili at lunch, or as a side with your collard greens and pork chops for dinner. It’s inexpensive, comforting, and seriously easy to make, with 8 pieces costing just $1.27 ($0.16 each)! So toss that boxed mix and let me show you how it’s done for real. 😉
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
“Perfect cornbread! My cornbread always turned out too dry and crumbly – no more! Moist but still with the bit of crumbly and lightness cornbread should have. Really like cooking it in a pie dish and having wedges as well. Thank you!”
Rebecca
A Humble Side with Staying Power
I originally made this cornbread back in 2015 to help stretch a pot of stew further during one of my budget challenges, and it’s been a favorite ever since. I make it completely from scratch with yellow cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, milk, an egg, and cooking oil, most of which you’ve probably already got in your cupboard or fridge! It’s as simple as whisking the wet ingredients, combining them with the dry ingredients, and baking. I don’t even use a mixer and there’s no rising time to worry about, either.
But what I love most about this classic recipe is that it’s lightly sweetened, sitting somewhere between the sweeter, almost cake-like cornbread’s and the more savory Southern-style versions. Just ¼ cup of sugar adds a little sweetness while still letting that lovely corn flavor come through. I also use regular milk instead of buttermilk (so there’s no need to buy a whole carton that you might struggle to use up!).
It’s a simple everyday side, but I love serving a slice alongside a Thanksgiving or Christmas roast, too. You can even bake it the day before, which means one less thing to worry about when you’ve got a big holiday meal to prepare!
Recipe Success Tips
- Use baking powder, NOT baking soda! They’re not interchangeable. This recipe uses baking powder because it contains the ingredients needed to give the cornbread a tender crumb and good rise. Baking soda used in its place can leave an unpleasant, bitter taste and won’t give the same rise or result.
- Mix gently for tender cornbread. I know it’s tempting to keep stirring until everything is completely smooth, but you don’t want to do that here! Overmixing can develop the gluten in the flour and make the finished bread a little rubbery. Stir until everything is moistened. A few lumps are perfectly fine.
- Use the baking dish you’ve got. This amount of batter fits well into an 8×8 casserole dish, 9-inch pie plate, or a 10-inch cast iron skillet (although you should preheat the skillet as the oven preheats). Glass, ceramic, and cast iron work best, but you can also use metal baking dishes.
- Prefer savory over sweet? You can reduce the sugar to suit your tastes. Some readers have even left it out completely with good results, although changing the sugar can affect the browning and texture slightly.
- Make corn muffins instead! This is a great option if you want individual servings or something easy to grab and pack for lunch. Pour the batter into an oiled muffin tin, filling each well about ¾ full. Bake at the same temperature (425°F) for 16-18 minutes, or until the tops are golden brown. I usually get about 10 corn muffins from one batch (see photo).
Three Ways to Avoid Dry Cornbread
A little crumbliness is part of cornbread’s charm, but it shouldn’t fall apart the moment you slice it. Too much flour or cornmeal, or leaving it in the oven too long, can quickly turn a moist crumb dry. Here’s how I help keep this recipe tender without losing that classic cornmeal texture:
- The flour adds structure, and the oil keeps things tender. Cornmeal doesn’t form gluten, so I use equal cups of all-purpose flour and cornmeal to help the bread hold together. Then the oil helps keep the crumb soft, even after it cools, because unlike butter, it stays liquid at room temperature.
- Measure your flour and cornmeal carefully. Too much of either can throw off the balance of wet and dry ingredients, leaving you with a dry and crumbly bread. I recommend weighing them with a kitchen scale for the most consistent results (140 g flour and 150 g cornmeal).
- Don’t overbake! This recipe takes about 20 minutes at 425°F, but the exact time can vary depending on your baking dish. Look for golden-brown edges and a golden top, then insert a toothpick into the center. It should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs (see photo below). There’s no need to keep baking once it’s done, or you risk drying it out.
What to Serve with Cornbread
Cornbread is a great side dish for any thick and hearty soup, stew, or chili. I especially love serving it with a big bowl of my classic chili. I’ll usually either dip a warm slice into the sauce or crumble it straight into my bowl (my favorite way to use up day-old leftovers!). The mild sweetness works really well with smoky spices and a little heat. But really, you can serve this recipe in place of your usual dipping bread with any soup or stew you love. It’s also delicious layered into an easy cornbread salad with beans, corn, and veggies for a potluck or gathering (recipe coming soon!)
I also love a warm slice with a pat of butter melting right on top. Add a drizzle of honey (as much or as little as you like!), and you’ve got a delicious afternoon snack with a cup of coffee or a sweet side for your eggs and bacon at breakfast.
And don’t forget about the holidays! I’d happily swap the usual dinner rolls for a slice of cornbread alongside some roasted turkey breast, a batch of my homemade cranberry sauce, and all the Thanksgiving fixings. You can also take it a step further and use this recipe to make our cornbread dressing, which is loaded with savory herbs and vegetables and makes enough to feed a crowd!
How to Make Cornbread from Scratch step-by-step photos
Preheat the oven and prepare your baking dish: Gather and measure your ingredients, then preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C/200°C fan/Gas Mark 7). Grease a 9-inch pie plate, 10-inch cast iron skillet, or 8×8-inch baking dish with non-stick spray (or butter for a little extra flavor). I’ve always loved using my glass pie dish, but this time we used cast iron, and any of these options will work.
Combine the dry ingredients: In a large bowl, stir together 1 cup (150 g) yellow cornmeal, 1 cup (140 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 tsp (9 g) baking powder, and ½ tsp salt. Make sure everything is well mixed so the baking powder is evenly distributed throughout.
Whisk the wet ingredients: In a separate bowl, whisk together 1 cup (240 ml) milk, 1 large egg, and ¼ cup (60 ml) cooking oil until the egg is fully broken up and everything is well combined.
Gently mix the batter: Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir just until everything is moistened and there are no dry pockets of flour. Don’t keep stirring until the batter is completely smooth. A few lumps are perfectly fine, and overmixing can make the finished bread a little rubbery.
Bake until golden brown: Pour the batter into your prepared dish and spread it evenly. Bake for about 20 minutes, or until the top and edges are golden brown.
The top may crack a little, and that’s perfectly normal! To check it’s done, insert a toothpick into the center. It should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cut into 8 pieces and serve. Enjoy!
More Cornbread Recipes to Try
- Give the classic recipe a cheesy, slightly spicy twist with my Chili Cheese Cornbread, made with cheddar, chili powder, and sweet corn kernels.
- I love combining two comfort food favorites in my Chili Cornbread Skillet. The homemade cornbread bakes right on top of a hearty bean chili, with a layer of melted cheddar in between!
- Mashed sweet potato, sour cream, cinnamon, and nutmeg make this Sweet Potato Cornbread extra moist, rich, and full of warm fall flavors.
Other Easy Classic Bread Recipes
Our Easy Homemade Cornbread recipe was originally published 9/5/15. It was retested, reworked, and republished to be better than ever 11/13/26.

articles.title: Xbox announces Wolfenstein 3
articles.body:
It’s been nearly a decade since Bethesda’s MachineGames released Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus in 2017, and now Xbox is ready to announce a sequel from the studio. Wolfenstein 3 was officially announced today, just days after Bethesda also confirmed that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel.
Xbox announces Wolfenstein 3
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed a new entry in the Wolfenstein series with a brief tease.
In a post, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the name and a photo of a script. “Looking forward to sharing more,” she said. MachineGames also announced the game in a post, saying the game is “in production” and sharing a photo from a motion-capture session. IGN reports that Brian Bloom (who plays protagonist William Joseph “BJ” Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (who plays Grace Walker) are reprising their roles, and they appear to be the featured actors in the photo.
The last mainline entry, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, launched in 2017 and continued the story of Blazkowicz in an alternate 1960s where Nazi Germany had won the Second World War. Wolfenstein: Youngblood also debuted in 2019 as a co-op spinoff, starring Blazkowicz’s twin daughters.

articles.title: Microsoft Outlook Goes Down Nationwide [UPDATE]
articles.body:
Microsoft Outlook Goes Down Nationwide [UPDATE] (variety.com) 145
			
		 	
				Microsoft is suffering a major Microsoft 365 outage that's disrupting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and SharePoint for users across the Americas, with more than 129,000 problem reports logged on Downdetector shortly after the disruption began. Microsoft blames the connectivity problems on an unexpectedly large number of unavailable servers that overloaded the remaining infrastructure. The company says it's redistributing traffic and restarting affected systems. From a report:  Microsoft was not providing an estimated time by which it expects service to return. Both individual Outlook users and those on enterprise accounts experienced problems logging in to the service. The outage also affected other Microsoft services, including Microsoft Teams, the Copilot 365 AI service and SharePoint Online. "Users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services," the company said on its Service Health Status page. 
UPDATE 11/12/26, 19:50 UTC: From Microsoft 365 Status: "We're testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are monitoring health as they return to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you."
UPDATE 11/12/26, 20:19 UTC: From Microsoft 365 Status: "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you.
UPDATE 11/12/26, 20:29 UTC: "According to https://downdetector.com/, much of the major services are down," writes Slashdot reader xocmot2. "AWS, Microsoft, Meta, on and on. Clearly not a Microsoft thing."
UPDATE 11/12/26, 6:17 UTC: Microsoft is still struggling to resolve the outage, which is confirmed to be global with disruptions reported across 74 countries and territories. The outage has disrupted businesses and government services in countries including Japan, Singapore, India, and Australia, while OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported related problems.
Microsoft says its recovery efforts have produced some improvements, but the fixes are not delivering "sustained recovery." Microsoft has ruled out a cybersecurity incident, and experts warn that the prolonged disruption could result in significant economic losses.

articles.title: ‘The end of Tesla!’: Cybertruck diehards turn on Elon Musk after he pulls the plug
articles.body:
The Cybertruck is heading to that shiny cyber-dumpster in the sky, leaving the folks who built online identities around Elon Musk’s polarizing pickup feeling bereft. Usually, Musk’s fanbase treads lightly around their idol’s mercurial decisions. This time, however, the truck’s demise has sparked rare backlash within the Tesla community — aimed squarely at the guy who signed its death warrant.
‘The end of Tesla!’: Cybertruck diehards turn on Elon Musk after he pulls the plug
Tesla’s polarizing pickup is heading to the scrap heap, leaving its biggest online boosters feeling betrayed and questioning Musk’s next big pivot.
Troy Meekhof, who posts on numerous social platforms under the moniker “The Cybertruck Guy,” has been vocal about his disappointment in Musk’s decision to wind down Cybertruck production by the end of summer 2027. (The original plan was to start winding down production in the spring, but then Musk decided to extend it a few months.)
In a 33-minute video on YouTube, Meekhof argues that Tesla never fully committed to making the Cybertruck a success, citing a lack of advertising, confusing pricing changes, and the decision to shift focus before the truck could fully establish itself in the market.
“It feels like they didn’t try to make Cybertruck a success,” he said.
He also had choice words for Musk’s reasons for ending the Cybertruck’s short run to make room at Giga Texas for the fully autonomous Cybercab: “Cancelling all of your best products... in favor of an autonomous platform that remains both software and regulatory constrained... seems like an absolutely terrible idea,” Meekhof vented.
The Cybertruck wasn’t the only Tesla product to meet an untimely end — at least according to those with stakes (and often stock options) in the company’s success. Earlier this year, Tesla discontinued the Model S and Model X, two of its flagship vehicles. With the end of the Cybertruck, Tesla is now left with just the Model 3 and Model Y as vehicles you can actually buy. (The Semi is strictly a commercial vehicle, while the Cybercab’s availability as a consumer product remains dubious, at best.)
“Cancelling Cybertruck after all the years of getting it to production to ‘make room for CyberCab’ is a lame excuse,” @TeslaXplored wrote on X. “There are like 500 CyberCabs in one city that only Tesla influencers are riding in. Taking away consumer cars instead of building what the people want will be the end of Tesla!”
He added, “Very sad what happened to Tesla over the last 5 years.”
Meanwhile, at least one prominent aftermarket company is offering to step in and pick up the mantle. Unplugged Performance, which makes aftermarket accessories, said it would produce the Cybertruck and other vehicles on the truck platform under license, with investors funding the effort: “Worth a conversation?”
Musk, for his part, seems less interested in litigating the particulars of Cybertruck production and more intent on selling a vision of Tesla’s future centered around the Cybercab and humanoid robots. “Cybercab will do a majority of all passenger miles in any jurisdiction where it is not prohibited by law,” Musk wrote on X earlier this week. “Obvious to anyone with eyes and a brain.”
He also pushed back on claims that the Cybertruck was killed because it was unprofitable. “The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate,” Musk said. “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”
To be sure, Cybertruck sales have been disappointing over its entire production run. Musk initially theorized that Tesla could sell 250,000-500,000 Cybertrucks annually, but the actual numbers have been far below those projections. Last year, Tesla is estimated to have sold around 20,000 trucks; the company is on track to sell fewer than that this year.
Whether Musk’s autonomous utopia pans out or ends up joining the Cybertruck in the vaporware graveyard remains to be seen. For now, the stainless-steel wedge that was supposed to be the ultimate symbol of an indestructible future has become a monument to Musk’s shifting attention span — and a stark reminder to Tesla’s most loyal boosters that in Elon’s world, nothing should be taken for granted.

articles.title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
articles.body:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years.
Intel, Microsoft and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from its leadership crisis.
As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel.
“Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch.
Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen.
The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.”
Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis, Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list.
Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away.
According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.”
Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips.
Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.”
And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s.
“These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said.

articles.title: I Never Cook a Thanksgiving Turkey Without This Crucial Tool
articles.body:
I Never Cook a Thanksgiving Turkey Without This Crucial Tool
There are a few pieces of oft-overlooked kitchen equipment that are nonnegotiable, in my opinion: a good chef’s knife, a kitchen scale, and, perhaps the most important, an instant-read thermometer. No one should be relying on unreliable advice like “when the juices run clear it’s done” to make sure their food is cooked thoroughly. It’s simply not foolproof, and when it comes to food safety I’m not interested in messing around.
The Thermapen Nano Beats Any Other Thermometer
Thermoworks is the cadillac of instant-read thermometers. Its Thermapen One has been our top pick for years, and multiple editors on our team also swear by the less spendy ThermoPop. The Thermapen Nano takes everything I loved about the Themapen One (accuracy, speed, usability, etc.) and improves upon it.
This updated model is faster, with a brighter display, and long-requested quality-of-life upgrades like a built-in magnet for convenient storage, and it comes with a 5-year warranty. The Thermapen Nano is intended to replace the Thermapen One in Thermoworks’ lineup. The Thermapen One will no longer be produced once existing inventory is gone. 
My Honest Review of the Thermapen Nano
I didn’t think it could get any better than the Thermapen One, which I have been using exclusively for over five years. I had no complaints about it. It’s reliable, wildly fast and accurate, durable, and easy to use.
What on earth would you improve? Thermoworks had answers for that question. After testing the Nano for over two months, I can say it’s definitely a worthy upgrade. 
It’s wildly fast.
The Thermapen Nano reads temperature even faster than the Thermapen One, which could accurately return results in one second. It’s so fast (0.4 seconds!) that I had trouble timing the readings manually. While that might not seem like a big deal, tell that to your hands when they’re in a hot oven trying to make sure the Thanksgiving turkey is cooked through.
It’s also, importantly, accurate. The Nano’s results are accurate to within +_0.5°F. I’ve never had an issue with accuracy with any Thermoworks thermometer I have used, although you should recalibrate your thermometer regularly, a ritual I have been guilty of putting off for too long in the past.
The display is even easier to read than before.
The Thermapen One had a backlit rotating display, and so does the Nano, but it’s 300% brighter, making temperatures easier to read than ever, even inside a dark oven. I didn’t realize how big of a difference the new display was until I sat my thermometers side by side. And while they’re both clear, the nano is undeniably easier to read.
It’s very easy to use.
When kitchen gear is thoughtfully designed, it rises to the level of almost ceasing to feel like a tool at all, becoming more like an extension of your arm (ask any chef about their favorite knife). The Nano boasts helpful features like integrated magnets that allow you to easily mount it to your stove, oven, or grill to keep it handy while cooking; it’s IP67 rated waterproof, so you can easily wash it in the sink; it’s less bulky than its predecessor; and it has a button on the back that allows quick switching between Fahrenheit and Celsius.
Buy: Thermapen Nano, $119, at Thermoworks
Why You Should Trust Me
I am a seasoned food editor who has been working in professional kitchens for almost 15 years. I have been using kitchen thermometers in both professional kitchens and in my home cooking that entire time. I’ve used everything from analog meat thermometers to high-end Bluetooth-enabled models and know what makes a thermometer reliable and worth its price tag. In addition to working as a chef and recipe developer, I’m a writer who has been testing and reviewing kitchen products for years.

articles.title: Whoop just launched a social network
articles.body:
Whoop, the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data.
The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us.
Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example.
I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention.
Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.
Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members.
He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.)
But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed.
As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls.
Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties.
He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health, a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.”
He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end.
As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty.
In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year.
As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band. But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

articles.title: A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem
articles.body:
Hi all,
the technical leadership committee of the Haskell Foundation has been successfully bootstrapped!
We have spent the last few weeks discussing our vision and strategy and are now fully operational.
We’re going to actively develop initiatives and proposals that we believe need funding and execution. For that we need companies, contractors and volunteers to help. Everyone can participate, whether it’s by dropping ideas informally, writing a concrete proposal themselves or finding entities that could support or fund initiatives.
We tried to keep the community proposal process as light as possible. However, we believe that fairness and participation are vital, especially when funding is involved, so anyone who writes a proposal should be aware that we will open the floor for the community to comment or even deliver counter-proposals. The process may evolve as we make experiences and get feedback.
Below is our vision. Feel free to get in touch with us!
The TLC’s shared vision
We believe that Haskell is awesome and that it can provide unique value to everyone, because it sits at an interesting intersection between human craftsmanship and machine automation:
- It is good for humans to write by hand: Type safety, powerful abstractions and referential transparency have enabled engineers all over the world in startups and big tech to deliver and maintain complex systems.
- It is good for responsible AI workflows: review is a significant bottleneck in modern AI-workflows and Haskell’s strengths heavily favor the reviewer. Additionally, the ability to quickly design eDSLs and express constraints where it matters allows to set up strong guardrails for code generation, without losing flexibility.
There may be better languages for formal verification or for vibecoding, but there’s no better language for “human in the loop”. Haskell is where we maintain control of our work, build institutional knowledge and ship responsibly.
We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone:
- Beginners: the onboarding experience must be our benchmark for usability
- Experts: enabling advanced workflows and improving productivity
- Industry: focussing on stability and scaling
A vision of productivity
Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance!
Iteration speed
Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows.
While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2.
Debugging and profiling
Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries:
- live step-through debugging
- actually useful stack traces
- beautiful performance analysis reports
And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP).
Debugging must be fun again, without littering Debug.Trace.trace all over your codebase.
Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools.
Onboarding and DevX
In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole.
- installation so quick that you’re wondering whether the installer even worked
- documentation so comprehensive and accessible that you never get stuck
- tooling so intuitive that you don’t have to constantly ask for support
This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as:
- write programs that do one thing and do it well
- write programs that work together
- write programs that are extensible
Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans.
A vision of a secure and trustworthy ecosystem
Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost.
To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to:
- have the fastest incident response time among language ecosystems
- have penetration testers go through our infrastructure regularly
- make end users aware of vulnerabilities and mitigations
- build a robust cryptography library stack
- harden our supply chain
We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of dependent types and liquidhaskell.
A vision of stability
What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes?
While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway.
The questions we need to answer along the way are:
- how can users opt out of breaking changes?
- how long can we keep support windows open?
- how can we make the upgrade experience better?
Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn.
We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem.
A vision of a flourishing open source ecosystem
All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other.
We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world.
We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values.

articles.title: Lonewolf 0.3 – A standalone XMPP server written in Rust
articles.body:
Repository navigation
Lonewolf v0.3.0 adds certificate-authenticated federation, direct TLS, and more desktop client features. It remains a pre-1.0, single-node server; full XMPP compliance and clustering remain on the roadmap.
Client and federation features
- Federation exchanges messages, IQs, presence, and roster subscriptions with other XMPP servers. Hosts with configured certificates and public DNS names federate by default. Peers need trusted certificates and SASL EXTERNAL; Server Dialback is not supported.
- Bidirectional connections (XEP-0288) let compatible servers share one connection. Stream Limits Advertisement (XEP-0478) exchanges federation stanza and idle limits.
- Direct TLS (XEP-0368) adds client and server listeners and combined STARTTLS/direct-TLS federation discovery.
- Private XML Storage (XEP-0049) stores private client settings and legacy bookmarks. Software Version (XEP-0092) answers domain software queries, with operating system disclosure off by default. Both extensions are enabled by default.
- Opt-in SCRAM-SHA-512 and SCRAM-SHA-512-PLUS implement an expired Internet-Draft, not an RFC or IANA-registered mechanism. Account creation and password changes write credentials older binaries cannot read, even when SHA-512 login is disabled.
The standards reference records supported roles and limits.
Operations and tooling
- Federation checks CA-published CRLs over plain HTTP by default. Downloaded checks allow unknown revocation status; s2s.tls.fetch_crls = false disables downloads. A configured s2s.tls.crls_path uses only the local file.
- letsencrypt.certificate_profile selects a CA-advertised profile, including short-lived certificates. Profile changes trigger early renewal.
- The default client stanza limit falls from 512 KiB to 256 KiB. Traffic byte counters now include TLS handshake and record overhead.
- The benchmark executable and crate are now lonewolfbench, replacing lonewolf-bench.
See the configuration reference for settings and defaults.
Build from source
Download and extract Source code (tar.gz) or Source code (zip) below, then run:
cargo build --release --locked -p lonewolf -p lonewolfctl -p lonewolfbench
Build on Linux or macOS with a stable Rust toolchain and a system linker. See the quick start for setup.
Full changelog: v0.2.0…v0.3.0.
License: Apache-2.0.

articles.title: Show HN: Reflota – Open-source data recovery for NTFS/FAT disks with phased copy
articles.body:
Recuperá archivos de discos, pendrives y tarjetas (NTFS, FAT32, FAT16, FAT12 y exFAT), incluso los que borraste. Gratis, de código abierto y en modo solo lectura.
Cuando Windows dice "el disco no está formateado", una carpeta no abre o el explorador se cuelga, muchas veces los archivos siguen ahí. Reflota los reconstruye leyendo el disco directamente: en NTFS lee toda la tabla maestra (MFT) y arma el árbol de carpetas con la información que cada archivo guarda de su propia carpeta; en FAT y exFAT lee las carpetas y sigue las cadenas de clusters.
También encuentra archivos borrados y te dice cuántos de ellos siguen recuperables. Y si el disco se formateó o ya no tiene nombres, puede buscar archivos por su contenido, encontrar particiones perdidas y hacer una copia segura de un disco que está fallando.
Estado: beta. Funciona, pero cada disco dañado es distinto. Probalo primero con una copia de lo importante si podés.
Novedades todavía sin probar en discos reales (se verificaron con imágenes de prueba, no con hardware): FAT16/FAT12, búsqueda de RAW de cámara/PSD/RAR, reconstrucción de JPEG fragmentados, buscador por nombre y copia por fases. Si probás alguna con un disco real, contá cómo te fue en Issues.
Bajá Reflota.exe desde la sección Releases. No necesita instalación ni Python.
Como el programa no está firmado digitalmente, Windows puede mostrar "Windows protegió su PC": tocá Más información → Ejecutar de todas formas. Algunos antivirus desconfían de los programas que leen discos de forma directa; el código es abierto y podés compilar el .exe vos mismo (ver más abajo). Junto a cada Release se publica el hash SHA256 para comprobar que la descarga no se corrompió.
- Abrí Reflota. Aparece la lista de tus discos y unidades.
- Tildá lo que querés recuperar, todo en el mismo árbol:
  - Tildar un disco o una partición → se copia todo.
  - Entrá en la partición y tildá solo carpetas o archivos → se copia solo eso.
  - El tamaño total se calcula solo mientras tildás.
  - Activá Incluir archivos borrados para ver también lo que se borró: aparece en rojo, en su carpeta original, con su estado.
  - Buscar por nombre (arriba del árbol): escribí parte del nombre (factura), un patrón (*.pdf, foto_??.jpg) y apretá Enter. Busca sin importar mayúsculas ni acentos, en la partición elegida (o en todas las que ya abriste), incluye lo borrado y muestra los resultados como un grupo nuevo del árbol que se tilda igual que lo demás. Primero abrí la partición (clic en su flecha).
- Abajo, elegí la carpeta donde copiar (en otro disco) y apretá RECUPERAR.
Podés parar cuando quieras y volver a empezar: lo que ya se copió no se repite.
Windows no deja leer un disco "en crudo" sin permisos de administrador (le pasa a cualquier programa de recuperación). Reflota abre sin pedirlos y los pide recién cuando tocás un disco para leerlo; ahí se reabre con el aviso de Windows. El programa nunca escribe en el disco de origen.
Elegí primero un disco o una partición en la lista.
Buscar archivos por contenido. Reconoce los archivos por su forma interna, sin necesitar nombres ni carpetas. Sirve cuando el disco se formateó, la tabla de archivos está destruida o el archivo borrado ya perdió su nombre. Podés buscar solo en el espacio libre (rápido, ideal para lo borrado) o en todo el disco o la partición. Los resultados aparecen en el mismo árbol, agrupados por tipo, y se recuperan igual que lo demás (tildar y RECUPERAR). Detecta: fotos (JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, WebP, HEIC, TIFF), fotos RAW de cámara (CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG, ORF, RW2, PEF, RAF), PSD/PSB de Photoshop, videos (MP4/MOV/3GP, AVI, MKV/WebM), audio (MP3, M4A, WAV), documentos (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, ODT/ODS/ODP, DOC/XLS/PPT, EPUB), comprimidos (ZIP, RAR, 7Z, JAR, APK) y bases de datos SQLite. El largo exacto de cada archivo se calcula leyendo su estructura (no se corta "a ojo"), y los archivos que contienen otros archivos adentro (como una miniatura en una foto) salen enteros. Los nombres originales no se pueden recuperar: salen numerados (recuperado_00012.jpg). Los archivos que estaban fragmentados (partidos en pedazos no contiguos) normalmente no se pueden rearmar y pueden salir incompletos o mezclados, salvo las fotos JPEG si tildás Reconstruir fotos JPEG fragmentadas: Reflota decodifica la foto hasta donde deja de ser válida y busca el pedazo que la continúa; solo la entrega si el resultado cierra exacto (todos los bloques de imagen y el final del archivo). Es mucho más lento, funciona con JPEG «baseline» (los de cámaras y celulares; no los progresivos) y puede no lograrlo cuando hay muchos fragmentos o el hueco está lleno de otras fotos parecidas: en ese caso la foto simplemente no aparece (no entrega una foto equivocada a propósito, pero conviene mirar el resultado).
Buscar particiones perdidas. Recorre el disco entero buscando los inicios de particiones NTFS, FAT32, FAT16/12 y exFAT, aunque la tabla de particiones esté borrada y hasta con los sectores de arranque destruidos (usa sus copias de respaldo). Las que encuentra se agregan a la lista. Puede tardar bastante en discos grandes y se puede parar.
Crear imagen del disco (copia segura). Cuando un disco falla, lo mejor es copiarlo una sola vez a un archivo y trabajar sobre esa copia, sin seguir forzando el original. La copia va por fases, como hacen las herramientas de rescate profesionales: primero lee rápido todo lo que se lee bien (saltando las zonas que fallan para no insistir), después recorta los bordes de las zonas dañadas, luego las lee sector por sector y al final reintenta los sectores ilegibles. Así se rescata lo máximo con el mínimo castigo al disco. Los sectores que nunca se pudieron leer quedan en ceros y se anotan en *.malos.txt. El avance se guarda en *.mapa: si se interrumpe (o se corta la luz) se continúa exactamente desde ahí. Después agregás la imagen a la lista y recuperás desde ahí.
- Dejá de usar el disco dañado. Cada escritura nueva puede pisar lo que querés recuperar.
- Copiá siempre a otro disco. Reflota se niega a copiar al mismo disco que está leyendo.
- Si el disco hace ruidos raros o desaparece a cada rato, apagalo: ese es un problema físico y conviene un servicio profesional.
Hace
- Lee discos físicos, unidades USB, tarjetas e imágenes de disco (.img).
- Sigue adelante aunque haya sectores ilegibles: los rellena con ceros, marca el archivo como parcial y lo anota en recuperacion_log.csv.
- Si el sector de arranque está dañado, prueba la copia de respaldo (FAT32, exFAT) y otras ubicaciones típicas de la MFT (NTFS). FAT16/FAT12 no guardan copia del arranque.
- Muestra los archivos que no encuentran su carpeta en _huerfanos.
Sobre los archivos borrados
- Al borrar un archivo, el sistema suele conservar su nombre y dónde estaba el contenido, pero libera ese espacio. Si después se guardaron otros archivos encima, el contenido se pierde. Reflota lo detecta y lo muestra como recuperable, N% intacto o sobrescrito (los sobrescritos no se copian; los parciales sí, avisando).
- NTFS: usa los registros libres de la MFT y el mapa de espacio libre ($Bitmap). Es lo más confiable.
- FAT32, FAT16/12 y exFAT: usa las entradas de carpeta borradas. Estos formatos borran la cadena de clusters, así que Reflota asume que el archivo estaba en un solo bloque seguido; si estaba fragmentado, el resultado puede salir mezclado aunque diga "recuperable". En FAT32, un archivo con nombre corto (formato 8.3) pierde la primera letra del nombre al borrarse (queda _orrame.pdf).
- Si el disco se formateó o la carpeta que lo contenía ya no existe, los borrados pueden aparecer en _borrados (carpeta de origen desconocida).
- Siempre conviene recuperar a otro disco y dejar de usar el original apenas se nota el problema.
No hace (todavía)
- No recupera otros sistemas de archivos como ext4, APFS o ReFS, ni discos con BitLocker sin descifrar.
- La búsqueda por contenido no reconstruye nombres, carpetas ni fechas, y solo sabe unir pedazos de fotos JPEG baseline (no otros formatos fragmentados).
- No detecta formatos muy poco comunes en la búsqueda por contenido, ni los PSD con compresión ZIP ni los JPEG progresivos fragmentados.
- Los archivos cifrados (EFS) o comprimidos por NTFS se omiten y quedan en el log.
- No repara el disco ni arregla fallas físicas.
reflota.exe --source \\.\PhysicalDrive5 --particiones
reflota.exe --source \\.\PhysicalDrive5 --offset 608174080 --ls /Programacion --borrados
reflota.exe --source \\.\PhysicalDrive5 --offset 608174080 --copiar /Programacion --dest D:\Recuperado
Con Python 3.8+ (Windows):
python reflota.py              # correr directo, sin instalar nada
.\build_exe.ps1                # genera dist\Reflota.exe
El .exe se publica sin firma. Para firmarlo hace falta un certificado de firma de código (se compra, o se pide gratis para proyectos de código abierto a servicios como SignPath Foundation). Con el certificado en un .pfx se firma así (requiere signtool del Windows SDK):
.\firmar_exe.ps1 -Pfx C:\ruta\certificado.pfx
El script incluido está sin probar (no se pudo verificar sin un certificado real). Aun firmado, SmartScreen puede avisar un tiempo hasta que el programa gane reputación.
MIT: usalo, copialo y modificalo libremente. Ver LICENSE.
Reflota is a free, open-source, read-only file recovery tool for NTFS, FAT32, FAT16/FAT12 and exFAT. On NTFS it reads the whole $MFT and rebuilds the folder tree from each file's parent reference; on FAT32/exFAT it walks the directories and cluster chains. It also lists deleted files in their original folders and tells you how much of each is still intact. One tree shows disks → partitions → folders: tick a disk to copy everything, or tick only what you want; the size is computed automatically. It has a name search (wildcards, accent-insensitive, includes deleted files). It can also carve files by content (30+ formats including camera RAW, PSD and RAR, with exact lengths read from their structure, plus an optional, slower reassembly of fragmented baseline JPEGs), find lost partitions even with destroyed boot sectors, and make a safe, phased, resumable image (ddrescue-style: easy areas first, then trim, scrape, retry) of a failing disk. Recent additions were verified on synthetic test images, not yet on real hardware. Never writes to the source disk. Windows requires administrator rights for raw disk access; Reflota starts without them and asks only when you open a disk. MIT licensed.

articles.title: Europe's electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow
articles.body:
Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.
Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.
Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
Europe’s growth keeps building
Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.
That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.
Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.
Germany’s EV share topped 45% of new car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.
UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.
And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.
North America’s rebound needs context
North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.
US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.
But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.
October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.
“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.
The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.
China’s EV share rises even as sales fall
China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.
Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.
Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.
Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.
Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.
Other markets grow fast, with some caveats
Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.
Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.
Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.
Top comment by fromEurope
Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.
As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.
Read more: Europe’s EV sales soar as North America drops 44% – here’s the catch

articles.title: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
articles.body:
The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.
That's about $500 above the last record, set in December 2025.
Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.
Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly.
While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.
"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.
The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.
It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds, a car analytics company.
Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.
"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.
Used cars are not a steal
The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.
It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.
The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive. Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.
Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.
That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.
But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.
No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.
A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.
The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.
"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.
Why are new cars so expensive?
In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.
But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.
American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.
Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.
For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.
Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."
"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."
A challenging time for automakers
Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.
And the market for car buyers is smaller. About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.
Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."
For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.
For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.
"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

articles.title: Don't argue with me. $100k is fair, and you know it
articles.body:
The first commercial product that I worked on after going on leave of absence from Apple in March 1984 (see Leave Of Absence) was a low cost, high resolution scanner for the Macintosh called Thunderscan, that I created in collaboration with a tiny company named Thunderware (see Thunderscan).  I started working on it in June 1984, and by early October, it was almost complete.
Tom Petrie, one of the two principals at Thunderware (the other was Victor Bull, who I worked with on the Silentype thermal printer 
(see What Hath Woz Wrought)
, the first project that I did for Apple), arranged a few demos for various computer magazines, to curry favorable reviews to promote the product.  On October 11th, 1984, I drove with Tom to an office in Hillsborough, to demonstrate Thunderscan for Byte magazine.
The Byte reviewer was John Markoff, a technology scribe for the San Francisco Chronicle who was one of the best reporters covering the personal computer industry.  Tom described Thunderscan while I set up the demo and started scanning.  John asked a few questions, taking notes with his IBM PC, which was running a character-based text editor that I viewed with the typical pious disdain of a Macintosh purist.  As I was answering one of his questions, the phone rang.
"Excuse me," he told us, as he pressed a key combination on his keyboard, his monitor screen instantly changing to a different program. (see Mea Culpa)

"OK, I've seen enough, " Steve interrupted me.  "It's great.  Apple is going to bundle it with the Mac.  Congratulations."
But then he paused, and stared at me for a moment with an incredibly intense gaze, as if he was sizing me up or maybe just trying to scare me.
"But I don't want you taking advantage of this situation.  I'm not going to allow you to take advantage of Apple."
"What do you mean?" I asked him, genuinely puzzled.
"There's no way that you could have written that program without confidential information that you learned by working at Apple.  You don't have the right to charge whatever you like for it."
I started to get angry. "The program is only half finished, and if I don't think you're paying me fairly, I won't be motivated to finish it."
Steve gave me another intense stare as he paused for a few seconds.  Then he stated a single number, without explanation.
"One hundred thousand dollars."
"I don't know," I told him, "I think it's probably worth a lot more than that."
"Don't argue with me.  $100,000 is fair, and you know it."
I didn't seem to have any alternative but to capitulate to Steve's price setting, since he's difficult to argue with and I really wanted Switcher bundled with the Mac. Getting Switcher going wasn't that hard, but it was a very difficult program to finish, because it overturned some of the underlying assumptions that applications were making, yet it was committed to keeping everything working anyway.  Much of the work in the latter stages involved testing it with every application that I could get my hands on and debugging crashes.  Usually I could concoct some kind of technique that would mitigate the problem without causing worse problems elsewhere.
Predictably, the hardest part of finishing Switcher was making it work smoothly with the Microsoft applications.  That was partially because Microsoft was a very early developer, and took liberties with the system that most developers would shy away from, but it was mostly because the instructions comprising their applications were encoded in pseudo-code to save space, in the tradition of the byte-code interpreters from Xerox, which Charles Simonyi advocated.
Unfortunately, the pseudo-code kept me from disassembling the program when it crashed, which made it more difficult to debug.  I finally developed a debugging technique by single stepping through their interpreter, six instructions at a time to get to the instructions that were doing the work,  but it was pretty painful.  I was determined to slog through it because of the promise that I made when I visited Microsoft.
One of the last problems that I addressed before finishing the first release of Switcher in March 1985 had to do with applications hanging.  If you're running multiple applications, you don't want one application hanging to take down all of them.   I added a feature that allowed the user to kill the current application if it was hung up, by monitoring for a specific key combination during the vertical blanking interrupt handler.
I knew that I had to pick a very rare key combination, because you didn't want users killing their applications accidentally.  I decided on shift-command-option-period, four keys held down at once, which I thought would be pretty hard to stumble into accidentally.   But I was surprised when I got a call from Jeff Harbers at Microsoft.
"Hey, I like that abort feature that you just added, but you're going to have to change the key combination, because we're using that in Microsoft Word.", Jeff told me.  Microsoft Word was very complex, and it possessed an enormous range of keyboard shortcuts, way too many, as far as I was concerned.
"OK, suggest something for me to change it to and I'll consider it," I told Jeff.
Jeff didn't have anything specific in mind, so he told me that he would get back to me soon.  I had to laugh when he called me back the next day, and told me that he wanted to withdraw his request and that I should keep shift-command-option-period as the abort sequence.
"OK, that sounds good to me, " I told him.  "But why the change?  Doesn't it still conflict with Word?"
"We'll change Word in the next release not to use it.  The problem was that we couldn't find a safe sequence - I guess we're already using every key combination!"
I officially released the finished version of Switcher in April 1985, and I maintained it for a few versions after that.  Eventually, I handed it off to Phil Goldman, a tremendous young programmer from Princeton who was recently hired at Apple, who went on to write MultiFinder (with Erich Ringewald), Switcher's eventual successor, in 1987.

Usually I could concoct some kind of technique that would mitigate the problem without causing worse problems elsewhere.
Predictably, the hardest part of finishing Switcher was making it work smoothly with the Microsoft applications.  That was partially because Microsoft was a very early developer, and took liberties with the system that most developers would shy away from, but it was mostly because the instructions comprising their applications were encoded in pseudo-code to save space, in the tradition of the byte-code interpreters from Xerox, which Charles Simonyi advocated.
Unfortunately, the pseudo-code kept me from disassembling the program when it crashed, which made it more difficult to debug.  I finally developed a debugging technique by single stepping through their interpreter, six instructions at a time to get to the instructions that were doing the work,  but it was pretty painful.  I was determined to slog through it because of the promise that I made when I visited Microsoft.
One of the last problems that I addressed before finishing the first release of Switcher in March 1985 had to do with applications hanging.  If you're running multiple applications, you don't want one application hanging to take down all of them.   I added a feature that allowed the user to kill the current application if it was hung up, by monitoring for a specific key combination during the vertical blanking interrupt handler.
I knew that I had to pick a very rare key combination, because you didn't want users killing their applications accidentally.  I decided on shift-command-option-period, four keys held down at once, which I thought would be pretty hard to stumble into accidentally.   But I was surprised when I got a call from Jeff Harbers at Microsoft.
"Hey, I like that abort feature that you just added, but you're going to have to change the key combination, because we're using that in Microsoft Word.", Jeff told me.  Microsoft Word was very complex, and it possessed an enormous range of keyboard shortcuts, way too many, as far as I was concerned.
"OK, suggest something for me to change it to and I'll consider it," I told Jeff.
Jeff didn't have anything specific in mind, so he told me that he would get back to me soon.  I had to laugh when he called me back the next day, and told me that he wanted to withdraw his request and that I should keep shift-command-option-period as the abort sequence.
"OK, that sounds good to me, " I told him.  "But why the change?  Doesn't it still conflict with Word?"
"We'll change Word in the next release not to use it.  The problem was that we couldn't find a safe sequence - I guess we're already using every key combination!"
I officially released the finished version of Switcher in April 1985, and I maintained it for a few versions after that.  Eventually, I handed it off to Phil Goldman, a tremendous young programmer from Princeton who was recently hired at Apple, who went on to write MultiFinder (with Erich Ringewald), Switcher's eventual successor, in 1987.

articles.title: Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
articles.body:
The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.
Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
A new look for the Humble Bundle storefront is missing an important security feature that was previously there.
However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.
