difference were also ported (see vendor/README.md).
Tatami, satin and short-stitch approaches follow Ink/Stitch.

articles.title: What’s really at stake in the Jensen Huang saga
articles.body:
One part of the saga surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ended on Thursday, when Huang resigned from his position at the top of AI’s most important company. But in the coming weeks and months, a much bigger story may be about to unfold. A story about Nvidia’s dealings in China, about the US government’s willingness to turn a lot of blind eyes to protect a powerful ally, and about the very stability of the AI industry as a whole. It’s a lot.
What’s really at stake in the Jensen Huang saga
On The Vergecast: The many spiraling stories in the AI world, the fate of streaming services, Mark Zuckerberg’s meat, and more.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay start by trying to unpack the many parts of the story. We’re all going to learn a lot more about Megaspeed than we ever planned or wanted, and we’re going to hear a lot of people — particularly newly elected Democrats — asking questions about who knew what and when. In the meantime, who will replace Huang as the AI industry’s front man? And will everyone survive the scrutiny that’s coming?
After that, the hosts tackle a week filled with small-ish news from streaming services that adds up to Hollywood’s plan to properly take on TikTok. We’re about to find out whether microdramas, free tiers, and a deep obsession with vertical video will save the Netflixes and Paramounts of the world. Will it work? Probably not. Is it the only rational thing to try? You bet. Finally, in the lightning round, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, Mark Zuckerberg’s AI experiments, the Cybertruck era, and more.
Watch | Listen | Get ad-free
In case you missed it this week: We also talked about private torrent trackers, reviewed the Apple HomeView, took your questions on the Vergecast Hotline, and discussed the Huang saga… a lot. And we want to hear all your thoughts about all of it! Call the Hotline at 866-VERGE11, send us an email at vergecast@theverge.com, and tell us everything that’s on your mind. And make sure you subscribe so you don’t miss an episode!

articles.title: NYC Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing'
articles.body:
The City Council passed a bill Thursday that bans companies in New York City from using surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data.
Surveillance pricing means shoppers see a price based on their personal data like demographics, credit, browsing history or purchasing history. The bill prohibits surveillance pricing both online and in stores, although the practice is mainly used on the web.
Speaker Julie Menin described surveillance pricing as an “insidious and predatory corporate practice” that erodes privacy and fairness.
“It's a practice that worsens the affordability crisis, and today it's a practice that we are going to be ending,” she said during a press conference ahead of the vote.
In one investigation cited by the Council, Target shoppers saw a jump in pricing based on location data showing whether they were inside or outside a store. Shoppers found that a 55-inch SmartTV cost $499 on the Target app when inside a store, and $599 when in the store parking lot.
Uber, Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing. Many of the companies have denied using the practice.
Under the bill, the city would be able to issue fines of up to $1,000 for each transaction that violates the ban.
Menin’s proposal follows legislation approved by Albany lawmakers in June that prohibits surveillance pricing online and in stores, with some exceptions.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement that he supports the ban. He called surveillance pricing “just another way corporations are finding to squeeze working people.”
“New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks,” he added.
Business groups have warned that the ban could hinder discounts or loyalty programs for customers.
“If enacted, this law will make it harder for small restaurants with limited marketing budgets to reach customers, putting them at a disadvantage against national chains,” said Josh Gold, a spokesperson for Uber.
The company operates Uber Eats, which allows restaurants to offer discounts based on search history and previous orders.
Menin said the legislation would not affect discounts.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
articles.body:
The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.
Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source, whatever happens next.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.
Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.
The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.
That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.
Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.
Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.
Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.

articles.title: IceWM
articles.body:
IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System. The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity, and not getting in the user’s way. It comes with a taskbar with pager, global and per-window keybindings and a dynamic menu system. Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse. Windows can be iconified to the taskbar, to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden. They are controllable by a quick switch window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list. A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable. Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama. IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented. It includes an optional external background wallpaper manager with transparency support, a simple session manager and a system tray. IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS, antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs.
Software
IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++. It is now maintained at Github.
Releases
The latest released version is 4.1.0 (2026-08-06).
Features
- Easy to use, simple and fast
- Standards compliant→
- Fully usable with keyboard
- Alt+Tab window switching
- Efficient resource usage
- Task bar (optional)
- Multiple workspaces
- Fully documented→
- A large number of themes→
- Usable with GNOME and KDE environments
- Regenerates menus when configuration changes
- Support for sound effects→
- Multiple focus modes
- Manual placement of windows option
- Autoraising of windows option
- Tooltips
- Configurable keybindings→
- Supports DockApps in a container
- Tabbed windows
Screenshots
The IceWM Screenshots Collection
Themes
IceWM is themeable.
The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme,
which is a collection of settings and small images.
Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org.
Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list.
Translations
IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there, then update.
Documentation
Bug Tracking
Report your icewm bugs on Github. Only report it once and give relevant details.
Install the latest release as follows
$ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ cd icewm-4.1.0
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
Install from unreleased development source code
Gettext must be installed.
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./autogen.sh
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
If you have cmake, an alternative is:
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix=/usr
$ cd build
$ sudo make install
Install package dependencies
To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script.
$ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh
$ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh
Verify package dependencies by:
$ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg
# or simpler:
$ ./rebuild.sh -d
More installation and configuration
Links
- IceWM Menuator for managing menu files with a GUI.
- IceWM sound files.
- IceWM release history.
- Compare window managers.
- List of all window managers and their helper programs.
- Extended window manager hints.
- The anatomy of the modern window manager (thesis).
License
IceWM is released under the terms of the GNU Library General Public License.
Donate
Contribute to ongoing development and support of IceWM by donating.

articles.title: Show HN: RealtimeVAD – trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech
articles.body:
Know that the speaker stopped, about 100 ms before Silero does.
RealtimeSTT · RealtimeTTS · Live demo · Spec · LiveKit plugin
A voice assistant can't do anything until it knows the user has stopped talking. Speech recognition, the LLM call and the voice output all wait for that one decision, and a normal voice activity detector takes a few hundred milliseconds to make it.
RealtimeVAD makes it sooner. It keeps Silero VAD to decide what is speech, and adds a second, faster check: every 10 ms it compares the audio level with the room's noise and with the speaker's own level. The moment the audio goes quiet, you get an event, long before Silero's probability has fallen.
- Input: 16 kHz mono audio in chunks of any size (float32, int16 or int16 bytes).
- Output: start, pause and end events, plus the audio of the running segment at any time.
- Lead: speech-off a median 100 ms before Silero's probability drops, and 206 ms before Silero's VADIterator reports the end, on 3,279 real turns. The end itself comes before Silero's in 82 % of turns, by a median 70 ms.
- Price: it also fires in short gaps between words, about ten times as often as Silero.
- Quiet input: a quiet speaker's soft word endings are not silence; on a noisy quiet line the lead is gone instead (details).
- Runs on: one CPU thread, far faster than realtime. Needs only numpy and onnxruntime; the Silero model is bundled, no torch.
- Status: alpha (0.0.5). The API may still change.
demo.mp4
The video uses a synthetic voice and shows a median lead of 92 ms. The 100 ms above is the median on real voice-assistant turns.
demo/ runs this page on your own microphone. It shows, turn by turn, how much sooner RealtimeVAD knew that you stopped than Silero alone, on the same audio.
pip install realtimevadfrom RealtimeVAD import VAD
vad = VAD()
for chunk in microphone_chunks():
    for event in vad.feed(chunk):
        if event.kind == "start":
            stream_to_asr(vad.audio())       # includes the audio just before speech began
        elif event.kind == "pause":
            speculate(vad.audio())           # the speaker may be done; this isn't the end yet
        elif event.kind == "end":
            finalize(event.segment.audio)
vad.audio() returns the running segment at any time, starting about 0.3 s
before the speech. end carries the finished segment with its audio, start
time, end time and the time the speech stopped.
If your assistant talks while the microphone is open, pass
vad.feed(chunk, playback=True) for those chunks so its own voice is handled
as possible echo. Every threshold and duration can be configured;
SPEC.md lists what is guaranteed.
pause is early and often wrong, on purpose. It fires on every breath, every
short gap between words and every stop consonant, so most pause events are
followed by more speech.
- Use it to start work you can cancel: finalize the transcript, call the
LLM, prepare the voice output. Cancel when speech continues. A wrong pause then costs almost nothing, and a right one saves hundreds of milliseconds.
- Never treat it as the end of the turn. Only end closes a segment.
- Can't cancel quickly? Ignore pause and wait for end. The extra
false alarms would cost you more than they save.
Change the import:
from silero_vad import load_silero_vad
from RealtimeVAD import VADIterator          # was: from silero_vad import VADIterator
vad_iterator = VADIterator(load_silero_vad(), sampling_rate=16000)
speech_dict = vad_iterator(chunk, return_seconds=True)   # {'start': ...} / {'end': ...} / None
The constructor and the results stay the same, but end arrives as soon as the
audio goes quiet. Without a model argument, it uses the bundled Silero model and
doesn't need torch.
livekit-plugins-realtimevad/
is a VAD plugin: realtimevad.VAD.load() in place of silero.VAD.load(). Its
README shows how the events map and what it measured against the Silero plugin
on the same audio. In short: against the Silero plugin's defaults the end of
speech comes about 380 ms sooner, but most of that is the shorter silence
setting (0.25 s instead of 0.55 s), which Silero can be given too. At the
same setting RealtimeVAD's end is 65 to 110 ms earlier, and LiveKit's turn
detector starts 95 to 180 ms earlier. Inside a LiveKit session the turn was
committed about 150 ms sooner than with Silero's defaults and about 70 ms
sooner than with Silero at 0.25 s.
Measured on 3,279 turns from a live voice assistant, each with its trailing
silence, with default settings. Silero's decisions are computed from the very
same frame probabilities, so both see identical input. "Speech-off" is
RealtimeVAD's last pause before the turn ended, against the first frame of
Silero's final run below its threshold.
Until 0.0.4 the first row read 110 ms. The 10 ms went into not cutting quiet speakers, see the next section.
The end event, against the end Silero's own silence count gives with the
same thresholds and the same 0.24 s (2,323 turns where both closed the same
segments inside the recording):
Up to 0.0.4 a single loud 10 ms block inside the quiet after a word (a click, a lip smack, a breath) stopped the quiet count for good and left the end to Silero. That happened in a third of 680 sampled turns. The count now starts again after it.
Reproduce with your own recordings (16 kHz mono WAVs, one turn each, with trailing silence):
python benchmarks/speech_off_lead.py <wav dir> out.json
Up to 0.0.4, "quiet" had a fixed floor (quiet_rms, about −54 dBFS). For a
speaker around −32 dBFS that is fine. For a quiet one (a phone line recorded at
source level, a distant microphone) the floor sits only a few dB under the
speech, their soft word endings counted as silence, and 0.24 s later the
segment ended while they were still talking. Since 0.0.5 the floor follows
the speaker: it is quiet_rms or 20 dB below the speaker's own level,
whichever is lower (floor_margin_db).
The same 3,401 turns, attenuated and sent through a simulated phone line (300–3400 Hz, 8 kHz, μ-law, line noise). "Ended while talking" counts turns with an end that the same detector does not make at the recorded level and that is followed by more speech. "Silero alone" is the same VAD with the quiet clock off, on the same audio.
What this says, and what it doesn't:
- Quiet speakers are no longer cut. Ends while the speaker talks and lost speech are now where Silero alone has them. In all of these runs RealtimeVAD's last end was never later than Silero's.
- A noisy quiet line has no lead. When the noise is less than about 20 dB below the speaker (the room-noise row, and the quiet phone line with its line noise), nothing can be called quiet without calling soft speech quiet. RealtimeVAD then ends where Silero does: correct, and no faster.
- Very quiet and narrowband speech is a Silero limit. At −62 dBFS, and on the phone line, Silero itself is unsure. Speech it never scores 0.9 used to start no segment at all (476 of the phone-line turns, 1,264 at −62 dBFS). The soft start halves that (186 and 380); Silero at its own 0.5 threshold still hears more (139 and 353). More turns found also means more ends counted in the phone rows. Amplifying such input before the VAD helps Silero most.
- Borderline endings. Ends with speech of the original recording inside the 0.24 s that counted as quiet are rarer than in 0.0.4 by a factor of 10 at −52 dBFS (1,970 turns then, 182 now), but restarting the count after a click added some back (141 without it). Ends followed by more speech and lost speech did not rise with it.
- The phone path is simulated, and the reference for "still talking" is the original wideband recording. One speaker, one microphone.
What to set:
python benchmarks/quiet_input.py <wav dir> out.json
Silero is less sure about quiet speech, most of all on a phone line: it finds
fewer turns and drops out inside them. VAD(normalize_to_dbfs=-30) amplifies
the frames Silero sees, by up to 20 dB and never into clipping, until speech
sits at −30 dBFS. Levels, the quiet clock and the audio you get back use the
input as it came. Same turns as above:
It is off by default because it is not free at normal level: 2 of 3,401 turns lost more than 100 ms, speech-off was earlier than Silero in 96 % instead of 98 % of turns, and in one phone-line turn the end came later than Silero alone. It needs Silero to score the speech 0.5 at least once before it acts, so the first quiet words of a stream can still be missed. On noisy quiet input the ends moved by more than the benchmark's "ended while talking" count can judge, so that count is not given here; borderline endings did not rise.
"mm-hmm", "yeah", "okay": 200 real ones from meeting recordings (AMI corpus,
close microphone, 0.15–0.8 s long). Up to 0.0.4, 50 of them were not reported
as speech at all: Silero scored 35 between 0.5 and 0.9, below the start
threshold, and 15 below 0.5. With the soft start 25 are missed, 15 of them
Silero's own. A start comes a median 160 ms after the word begins. Whether
such a sound is a backchannel, a turn or an interruption is not a VAD
question and not answered here.
- The numbers come from one speaker and one capture chain: browser capture with noise suppression and echo cancellation, mostly quiet rooms.
- The lead needs audio that actually goes quiet after a word, and noise suppression helps that. In the 137 noisier turns (room level above −70 dBFS) the median lead was 102–124 ms. Without noise suppression in a loud room, expect less; with noise within about 20 dB of the speaker, none.
- Earlier is not the same as correct: at the recorded level, whether a speech-off sometimes lands inside a soft word ending was not checked against word timings. The quiet-input table above checks it against the same audio at normal level.
- The 100 ms are for speech-off. end waits 0.24 s after speech-off in both
cases; its own gain over Silero is smaller (a median 70 ms, none in 18 % of
turns) and depends on the noise.
- Whisper is mostly not detected (Silero scores it below 0.5). Laughter, coughs and sneezes often are.
- A DC offset in the input hides the silence from the quiet clock: no early end then, nothing lost.
- 16 kHz mono only.
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest
The edge-case tests in tests/audio/ run on about 100 MB of freely licensed
audio that is not in git (speech in 8 languages, noise, music, coughs and
laughter, whisper, real backchannels and hesitations). Without it they are
skipped. To get it (about 1.3 GB of downloads, checked by sha256):
python tests/audio/fetch_audio.py
python tests/audio/fetch_backchannels.py
pytest tests/audio
They take about 10 s with 8 worker processes and print what each test guards, with the measured value and its limit. Sources and licenses: LICENSES-audio.md, LICENSES-backchannels.md.
MIT. The bundled speech model is Silero VAD (MIT).

articles.title: Jensen Huang was having a third affair, Reuters reports
articles.body:
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was having a separate affair with an employee that has not been previously reported, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Huang stepped down as CEO and board member for the company earlier today, in the wake of news of extramarital affairs with accused spy Alice Huang and Nvidia VP of Healthcare Kimberly Powell. CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO, but no permanent successor has been named.
Reuters is withholding the name of the new employee linked to Huang but says she is an employee of Nvidia.
Huang has been called before Congress to testify about the national security implications of his relationship with Alice Huang in the coming weeks — but it’s unclear how much more will be revealed before the hearings take place. Already, his abrupt fall from grace is expected to have significant repercussions for the industry at large.
